Graph-Theoretic Formulation of Hamiltonian and Ground-State Sign Structures in Heisenberg Antiferromagnets

Mahmud Ashraf Shamim Email: mashamim@crimson.ua.edu Affiliation: Department of Physics and Astronomy, University of Alabama, Tuscaloosa, 35487, Alabama, USA    Md Moshiur Rahman Raj Email: moshiur_rahman@tutanota.com Affiliation: Department of Physics, University of Rajshahi, P.O. Box 6205, Rajshahi, Bangladesh    Mohamed Hibat-Allah Affiliation: Department of Applied Mathematics, University of Waterloo, Ontario Canada N2L 3G1 Affiliation: Vector Institute, Toronto, Ontario, M5G 0C6, Canada    Ruy Fabila-Monroy Affiliation: Departamento de Matemáticas, Cinvestav, Mexico    Nobuchika Okada Affiliation: Department of Physics and Astronomy, University of Alabama, Tuscaloosa, 35487, Alabama, USA    Paulo T. October 21, 2026
Abstract

We study Heisenberg antiferromagnets through a graph-theoretic representation of their Hamiltonians. In the computational basis of a fixed-magnetization sector, the Heisenberg Hamiltonian equals a constant minus the weighted Laplacian of a graph whose vertices are spin configurations and whose edges connect configurations related by exchanging two antiparallel spins on a lattice bond. We call this graph the Hilbert graph (HG) which is isomorphic to the token graph of the lattice over which the Hamiltonian is defined. The exact ground-state energy is then determined by the largest eigenvalue of the HG Laplacian, which is the spectral relaxation of weighted Max-Cut on the HG. With the amplitudes fixed, the phase-dependent part of the variational energy defines an antiferromagnetic classical XY model on the HG, with couplings set by the amplitudes. Restricting the variational state to be real, i.e., restricting its phases to {0,π}\{0,\pi\}, reduces the fixed-amplitude energy minimization to solving an antiferromagnetic Ising model and hence a weighted Max-Cut on the HG. When the weights are generated from non-degenerate ground-state amplitudes, the optimal phases give the ground-state sign structure which can be recovered from the weights in time polynomial in the size of the HG. On the Hamiltonian side, a diagonal sign transformation removes all positive off-diagonal matrix elements if and only if the HG is bipartite, which reproduces the Marshall sign rule on bipartite lattices through the graph two-coloring problem; otherwise, the minimal remaining positive weight equals the sum of HG edge weights left uncut by the Max-Cut. This graph formulation establishes a common framework for understanding wave function sign structure, Hamiltonian stoquasticity, non-convexity of phase optimization in variational Monte Carlo, and the average sign in quantum Monte Carlo.

I Introduction

Geometrically frustrated Heisenberg antiferromagnets (HAFs) remain a central challenge in quantum magnetism. Frustration prevents all exchange interactions from being satisfied simultaneously, which produces strong competition among low-energy states. Exact ground states are known only in a few special cases, most notably the dimer-product state at the Majumdar–Ghosh point [39, 40] and the dimer phase of the Shastry–Sutherland model [64]. Consequently, our understanding of these systems has largely relied on variational methods for ground state (GS) computation, including the density-matrix renormalization group [76, 60], tensor networks [48], and variational Monte Carlo (VMC) [5], and the difficulty of studying frustrated HAFs is closely tied to the limitations of these methods.

In VMC, a wavefunction ansatz is optimized using energy and gradient estimates from configurations sampled according to its Born distribution [5]. If amplitudes and phases are both trainable, VMC learns them together to approximate the GS. These ansätze broadly fall into three classes [33]: physics-based forms such as Gutzwiller-projected states [23], Jastrow-correlated states [27], and Pfaffian wavefunctions [44]; neural quantum states (NQS) [12], in which a neural network represents the wavefunction; and hybrids of the two [47, 20]. Among the three classes, NQS are distinguished by universal approximation [15, 26]: a sufficiently large network can represent any function, and corresponding expressibility results have been established for many-body quantum states [17, 21]. NQS can therefore represent both the amplitudes and signs of the GS wavefunction in principle, but universal approximation theorems do not let us predetermine the network size, nor do they guarantee accurate sign learning through variational optimization. In frustrated HAFs, it has been observed that learning the signs is considerably harder than learning the amplitudes [74, 8, 66]. In practice, accuracy often improves for various NQS architectures [25, 45, 57, 14, 13, 55, 35, 63], when the sign structure is supplied explicitly as a sign prior, most commonly the Marshall sign rule (MSR) [41]; in hybrid ansätze, the prior is supplied by a pair-product factor and optimized alongside the amplitudes [47, 20].

Many of these architectures have been benchmarked on the square lattice J1J_{1}–J2J_{2} HAF. At J2=0J_{2}=0, the MSR gives the exact GS sign structure, and it remains a good approximation for small J2J_{2} [54]. In the strongly frustrated window J2/J1≈0.5J_{2}/J_{1}\approx 0.5 to 0.60.6, however, no reliable sign prior is known, and performance at J2/J1=0.5J_{2}/J_{1}=0.5 has become the benchmark by which NQS architectures are judged. Table I of Ref. [52] compares variational energies on the 10×1010\times 10 square lattice at this point: most of the ansätze listed there use the MSR, while the Deep Vision Transformer [52] and group convolutional network [56] reach competitive energies without it, as do several architectures on the triangular and other frustrated lattices [69, 70, 53, 71, 30]. Architectural design can therefore ease the learning of the GS sign structure, but it does not explain what makes that structure hard to learn.

Because NQS training is largely a black box, understanding the origin of this difficulty is important for further progress on frustrated HAFs. A few studies have tried to explain this through complexity. Westerhout et al. [75] fixed the GS magnitudes at their exact-diagonalization values and mapped sign reconstruction onto an auxiliary classical Ising model. For the frustrated HAFs they studied, the induced Ising models had non-glassy optimization landscapes, and a greedy algorithm recovered the signs accurately. Schurov et al. [61] analyzed the Boolean Fourier spectra of GS sign structures and showed that several spectral features correlate with learning difficulty. Both studies suggest that sign-learning difficulty is encoded in an identifiable structure of the GS signs; what determines this structure, however, has remained unaddressed.

In this work, we study the HAF in a graph-theoretic framework. In a fixed-magnetization sector, the computational-basis configurations form the vertices of a weighted graph in which two configurations are joined by an edge whenever the Hamiltonian has a nonzero off-diagonal element between them, with that element as the edge weight. Westerhout et al. [75] defined their auxiliary Ising model on this graph, restricted to a subset of the basis. We call it the Hilbert graph (HG), since its vertices form a basis of the sector Hilbert space. We show that the HG is the token graph of the underlying lattice [19]. This identification lets us explain several results related to the sign structure of the variational wavefunction and the HAF Hamiltonian. The main contributions of this work are as follows.

  • •

    Any odd cycles in the HG follow from the odd cycles of the physical graph on which the HAF is defined. On a bipartite HG, the two-coloring gives the MSR, while odd cycles in non-bipartite HG obstruct the construction of any sign assignment that satisfies antiferromagnetic alignment on every edge.

  • •

    Building on the correspondence between the Heisenberg Hamiltonian and the token-graph Laplacian [49, 3], we write Hℓ=EF​I−LℓH_{\ell}=E_{F}I-L_{\ell} for the J1J_{1}–J2J_{2} HAF. Here HℓH_{\ell} is the Hamiltonian restricted to sector ℓ\ell, EFE_{F} is the fully polarized energy, II is the identity matrix and LℓL_{\ell} is the coupling-weighted HG Laplacian. We show that computing the GS energy is equivalent to solving a spectrally relaxed Max-Cut on the HG, in which the signs act as classical Ising spins situated at the vertices of the HG.

  • •

    The S​U​(2)SU(2) invariance of the Heisenberg Hamiltonian yields the following results on the HG Laplacian spectrum: the ladder operators S^tot±\hat{S}^{\pm}_{\rm tot} connect the eigenvectors of Laplacians of neighboring sectors, so the Laplacian spectrum of the HG in sector ℓ−1\ell-1 is contained in that of sector ℓ\ell for ℓ≤N/2\ell\leq N/2. This provides a physical explanation for a known result on token graph Laplacian spectrum [16, 3] and demonstrates that quantum mechanics is a valid way to study the token graph Laplacian. The result also implies that, for an even number of spins, the GS is attained in the zero-magnetization sector.

  • •

    At fixed amplitudes, the phase-dependent energy is an amplitude-dressed XY model on the HG, and binary phases reduce it to a weighted Max-Cut on HG. For a nondegenerate GS, the Goemans–Williamson relaxation [22] reproduces the GS signs exactly in time polynomial in the size of the HG, providing a rigorous counterpart to some of the observations used by Westerhout et al. [75] to conclude that the energy landscape is non-glassy and very mildly frustrated.

  • •

    When amplitudes and phases are parameterized by different sets of variational parameters, VMC acts as an evolving Rank-2 [11] relaxed Max-Cut, whose nonconvex landscape the phase ansatz inherits. This correspondence with the Rank-2 relaxation method also offers a possible explanation for why sign optimization is easier on bipartite lattices, without imposing MSR as a prior.

  • •

    The same odd cycles in non-bipartite HG that prevent antiferromagnetic sign alignment on all edges, also prevent any real diagonal unitary transformation from making the HAF Hamiltonian stoquastic.

  • •

    The average sign, the ratio of the sector partition function to that of its sign-free counterpart, is given by a temperature-dependent Estrada spectral bipartivity [18] of the HG that retains the Hamiltonian’s diagonal part.

This HG structure has appeared independently in several contexts. Related constructions include double-vertex graphs [1], symmetric graph powers [4], quantum-inspired graph invariants [58], superlattices [46], and token graphs [19]. Osborne [49] related the XY and Heisenberg Hamiltonians in fixed-magnetization sectors to adjacency and Laplacian operators on graph wedge products, and Ouyang [50] used symmetric products to bound the Heisenberg ferromagnet’s spectrum. None of these studies addressed the sign structure of the many-body wavefunction, which we study here.

The paper is organized as follows. Section II introduces the HG formulation of the HAF, and Section III studies its structure. Section IV connects the GS energy functional to a relaxation of Max-Cut, while Sec. V discusses optimization methods. Section VI analyzes the non-convexity of the VMC optimization landscape for a particular type of ansatz. In section VII, we show the relation between the stoquastic Hamiltonian and HG Max-Cut, and in section VIII establish the relation between the average sign in quantum Monte Carlo and the Estrada bipartivity. Section IX is for the conclusion and outlook.

II Hilbert Graph Formulation of the HAF

In this section, we show that the computational-basis configurations of a HAF in each fixed-magnetization sector carry a graph structure and study its basic structural properties. We then show that, after a constant energy shift, the sector Hamiltonian is the negative weighted Laplacian of this graph.

II.1 Hilbert Graph Construction

We represent the physical lattice by a finite, simple, undirected connected graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E), where VV and EE are the vertex and edge sets, respectively, and N=|V|N=|V| is the number of vertices. Each vertex i∈Vi\in V carries a spin-12\tfrac{1}{2} degree of freedom 𝐒^i=12​𝝈^i\hat{\mathbf{S}}_{i}=\tfrac{1}{2}\hat{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_{i}.

We consider the J1J_{1}–J2J_{2} Heisenberg antiferromagnet (HAF), in which the edge set decomposes as E=E1⊔E2E=E_{1}\sqcup E_{2}, where E1E_{1} and E2E_{2} are fixed by the lattice geometry and contain the nearest-neighbor (NN) and next-nearest-neighbor (NNN) bonds, respectively. We therefore write the graph GG in terms of its NN and NNN spanning subgraphs as

G=⋃r=12Gr,Gr=(V,Er).G=\bigcup_{r=1}^{2}G_{r},\quad G_{r}=(V,E_{r}).

Here G1G_{1} is the NN graph, G2G_{2} is the NNN graph, and GG is the full interaction graph. Edges in E1E_{1} carry coupling J1J_{1}, while edges in E2E_{2} carry J2J_{2}. For antiferromagnetic couplings J1,J2>0J_{1},J_{2}>0, the Heisenberg Hamiltonian is

H^=J1​∑{i,j}∈E1𝐒^i⋅𝐒^j+J2​∑{i,j}∈E2𝐒^i⋅𝐒^j.\hat{H}=J_{1}\sum_{\{i,j\}\in E_{1}}\hat{\mathbf{S}}_{i}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{S}}_{j}+J_{2}\sum_{\{i,j\}\in E_{2}}\hat{\mathbf{S}}_{i}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{S}}_{j}. (1)

We now separate H^\hat{H} into its diagonal Ising part and off-diagonal exchange part, H^=H^c+H^q\hat{H}=\hat{H}_{c}+\hat{H}_{q}, where

H^c\displaystyle\hat{H}_{c} =∑r=12Jr​H^rz​z,\displaystyle=\sum_{r=1}^{2}J_{r}\,\hat{H}^{zz}_{r},\quad H^rz​z\displaystyle\hat{H}^{zz}_{r} =∑{i,j}∈ErS^iz​S^jz,\displaystyle=\sum_{\{i,j\}\in E_{r}}\hat{S}^{z}_{i}\hat{S}^{z}_{j}, (2)
H^q\displaystyle\hat{H}_{q} =∑r=12Jr2​H^r±,\displaystyle=\sum_{r=1}^{2}\frac{J_{r}}{2}\,\hat{H}^{\pm}_{r},\quad H^r±\displaystyle\hat{H}^{\pm}_{r} =∑{i,j}∈ErS^i+​S^j−+S^i−​S^j+.\displaystyle=\sum_{\{i,j\}\in E_{r}}\hat{S}^{+}_{i}\hat{S}^{-}_{j}+\hat{S}^{-}_{i}\hat{S}^{+}_{j}. (3)

Here H^rz​z\hat{H}_{r}^{zz} is diagonal in the computational basis, while the off-diagonal term exchanges an antiparallel pair, (↑i↓j↔↓i↑j)(\uparrow_{i}\downarrow_{j}\leftrightarrow\downarrow_{i}\uparrow_{j}), on a bond in ErE_{r}. We refer to this elementary exchange as a Heisenberg flip (HF).

We label each state by a spin configuration σ∈{↓,↑}N\sigma\in\{\downarrow,\uparrow\}^{N}. We denote the spin at ii’th coordinate of σ\sigma as σ(i)\sigma^{(i)}. If a single HF on a bond {i,j}\{i,j\} in ErE_{r} transforms σ\sigma into τ\tau, we refer to τ\tau as a range-rr neighbor of σ\sigma. We use the notation σ​⇌i​j​τ\sigma\overset{ij}{\rightleftharpoons}\tau to refer to the fact that exchanging spins of sites ii and jj changes σ\sigma to τ\tau and vice versa. The set of range-rr neighbors of σ\sigma HF is then

𝒩r​(σ)={τ:σ​⇌i​j​τ​ for ​{i,j}∈Er}.\mathcal{N}_{r}(\sigma)=\{\tau:\sigma\overset{ij}{\rightleftharpoons}\tau\text{ for }\{i,j\}\in E_{r}\}. (4)

Since a single HF changes two sites, the pair {σ,τ}\{\sigma,\tau\} determines the flipped physical bond {i,j}\{i,j\} uniquely. Because E1∩E2=∅E_{1}\cap E_{2}=\emptyset, the induced sets are also disjoint: 𝒩1​(σ)∩𝒩2​(σ)=∅\mathcal{N}_{1}(\sigma)\cap\mathcal{N}_{2}(\sigma)=\emptyset. We define the set of all range-rr neighbors as

𝒩⁡(σ)=⨆r=12𝒩r​(σ).\mathcal{N}(\sigma)=\bigsqcup_{r=1}^{2}\mathcal{N}_{r}(\sigma).

HFs conserve S^totz=∑i∈VS^iz\hat{S}^{z}_{\mathrm{tot}}=\sum_{i\in V}\hat{S}^{z}_{i}, or equivalently the number of up spins in a spin configuration σ\sigma, which we denote by n↑​(σ)n_{\uparrow}(\sigma). Two basis states can therefore be joined by an HF only if they carry the same value of n↑​(σ)n_{\uparrow}(\sigma). For HAFs, n↑n_{\uparrow} is related to the magnetization mm by

n↑​(σ)=m⁡(σ)+N2,m⁡(σ)=⟨σ|S^totz|σ⟩.n_{\uparrow}(\sigma)=m(\sigma)+\frac{N}{2},\quad m(\sigma)=\braket{\sigma|\hat{S}^{z}_{\mathrm{tot}}|\sigma}. (5)

Fixing n↑​(σ)=ℓn_{\uparrow}(\sigma)=\ell gives a magnetization sector that is closed under HFs,

𝒱ℓ={σ∈{↓,↑}N:n↑(σ)=ℓ},ℓ=0,1,⋯,N.\mathcal{V}_{\ell}=\left\{\sigma\in\{\downarrow,\uparrow\}^{N}:n_{\uparrow}(\sigma)=\ell\right\},\quad\ell=0,1,\cdots,N. (6)

The range-rr edges inside this sector are

ℰℓ,r={{σ,τ}:σ∈𝒱ℓ​ and ​τ∈𝒩r​(σ)}.\mathcal{E}_{\ell,r}=\{\{\sigma,\tau\}:\sigma\in\mathcal{V}_{\ell}\text{ and }\tau\in\mathcal{N}_{r}(\sigma)\}. (7)

These edge sets are also disjoint, ℰℓ,1∩ℰℓ,2=∅\mathcal{E}_{\ell,1}\cap\mathcal{E}_{\ell,2}=\emptyset. We write the full edge set in sector ℓ\ell as

ℰℓ=⨆r=12ℰℓ,r.\mathcal{E}_{\ell}=\bigsqcup_{r=1}^{2}\mathcal{E}_{\ell,r}. (8)

Therefore, by fixing the number of up spins, we can define a graph through HFs on the vertices. We call this the Hilbert graph (HG) of the J1J_{1}–J2J_{2} HAF in sector ℓ\ell, and represent it as

Γℓ​(G)=(𝒱ℓ,ℰℓ)\Gamma_{\ell}(G)=(\mathcal{V}_{\ell},\mathcal{E}_{\ell}) (9)

Because each sector is closed under the HF operation, the full computational-basis HG is the disjoint union of the sector graphs,

Γfull​(G)=⨆ℓ=0NΓℓ​(G).\Gamma_{\rm full}(G)=\bigsqcup_{\ell=0}^{N}\Gamma_{\ell}(G). (10)

Since different sectors share no vertices, we may analyze each Γℓ​(G)\Gamma_{\ell}(G) independently. For a physical graph GG with NN vertices, a vertex of Γℓ​(G)\Gamma_{\ell}(G) is a choice of ℓ\ell sites carrying up spins. Thus |𝒱ℓ|=(Nℓ)|\mathcal{V}_{\ell}|=\binom{N}{\ell} and ∑ℓ=0N|𝒱ℓ|=2N\sum_{\ell=0}^{N}|\mathcal{V}_{\ell}|=2^{N} is the total number of computational basis states. Hence, for a fixed-ℓ\ell sector, the number of HG vertices counts the dimension of the Hilbert space in that sector.

The fully down-polarized state |↓,⋯,↓⟩\ket{\downarrow,\cdots,\downarrow} is the unique vertex of Γ0​(G)\Gamma_{0}(G), and we take this as the reference state. A configuration with ℓ\ell up spins carries ℓ\ell magnons above this vacuum. The first nontrivial case is the one-magnon sector, for which

Γ1​(G)≅G.\Gamma_{1}(G)\cong G. (11)

For fixed ℓ\ell and large NN, one has

(Nℓ)∼Nℓ/ℓ!.\binom{N}{\ell}\sim N^{\ell}/\ell!.

Thus the one-magnon HG has NN vertices, while the two-magnon HG has 𝒪⁡(N2)\mathcal{O}(N^{2}) vertices. More generally, if ℓ\ell is held fixed as NN grows, the HG grows only polynomially with system size. At finite magnon density, α=ℓ/N\alpha=\ell/N with 0<α<10<\alpha<1, Stirling’s approximation gives

(Nα​N)∼eN​h​(α)2​π​N​α​(1−α),\binom{N}{\alpha N}\sim\frac{e^{Nh(\alpha)}}{\sqrt{2\pi N\alpha(1-\alpha)}},

where h⁡(α)=−α​ln⁡α−(1−α)​ln⁡(1−α)h(\alpha)=-\alpha\ln\alpha-(1-\alpha)\ln(1-\alpha). Thus, HGs at finite magnon density grow exponentially with NN. The largest sector is the zero-magnetization sector where ℓ=N/2\ell=N/2.

Intermediate scalings of ℓ\ell give intermediate growth. For example, when ℓ∼N\ell\sim\sqrt{N}, the HG size grows faster than any power of NN but slower than exp⁡(c​N)\exp(cN) for fixed c>0c>0. Thus, the scaling depends on the sector: fixed-ℓ\ell sectors grow polynomially, whereas sectors with ℓ=α​N\ell=\alpha N grow exponentially. The exponential growth is largest near the center of the magnetization tower. Moreover, a global spin flip maps the ℓ\ell sector to the (N−ℓ)(N-\ell) sector, giving the duality

Γℓ​(G)≅ΓN−ℓ​(G).\Gamma_{\ell}(G)\cong\Gamma_{N-\ell}(G). (12)

For even NN, the self-dual sector is ℓ=N/2\ell=N/2, which coincides with the zero-magnetization sector. Fig. 1 illustrates the construction of ΓN/2​(G)\Gamma_{N/2}(G) for a six site chain J1J_{1}–J2J_{2} HAF.

The HG is built from the nonzero off-diagonal matrix elements of the Hamiltonian H^\hat{H} in Eq. (1), so both its vertex set and its connectivity depend on the basis in which it is written. We have worked throughout in the computational basis, which lets us identify it as a token graph [19].

In a fixed magnetization sector ℓ\ell, represent each up spin by a token and each down-spin site by an unoccupied vertex of GG. A configuration σ∈𝒱ℓ\sigma\in\mathcal{V}_{\ell} is then a placement of ℓ\ell indistinguishable tokens on VV. An HF acts only on an antiparallel pair, so along a bond {i,j}∈E\{i,j\}\in E it moves a single token onto an adjacent unoccupied vertex and leaves every other token where it is. This is the adjacency rule of the ℓ\ell-token graph Fℓ​(G)F_{\ell}(G) [19]. Hence,

Γℓ​(G)≅Fℓ​(G),\Gamma_{\ell}(G)\cong F_{\ell}(G), (13)

where Fℓ​(G)F_{\ell}(G) denotes the ℓ\ell-token graph of GG. Restricting the HFs to bonds in E1E_{1} or E2E_{2} gives

Γℓ​(G1)≅Fℓ​(G1),Γℓ​(G2)≅Fℓ​(G2).\Gamma_{\ell}(G_{1})\cong F_{\ell}(G_{1}),\qquad\Gamma_{\ell}(G_{2})\cong F_{\ell}(G_{2}).

The same correspondence therefore holds for the NN and NNN interaction graphs separately. The relation Γ1​(G)≅G\Gamma_{1}(G)\cong G is the ℓ=1\ell=1 case, since F1​(G)≅GF_{1}(G)\cong G.

Under a general unitary transformation, the matrix elements of H^\hat{H} may be mixed, and the resulting HG need not have the connectivity of Fℓ​(G)F_{\ell}(G). The token graph therefore serves as the bare HG, the structure the HAF carries before any basis transformation. Sec. VII discusses basis transformations, where the diagonal unitary transformations preserve the HG connectivity and hopping magnitudes, changing only the signs of the corresponding off-diagonal matrix elements. Identifying the HG as the token graph lets us express the Hamiltonian in terms of the graph Laplacian, which we discuss next.

II.2 Hamiltonian as the Hilbert Graph Laplacian

At the operator level, the exchange term in Eq. (3) acts as the adjacency operator on the HG. For each range rr, H^r±\hat{H}_{r}^{\pm} connects exactly those configurations joined by an edge in ℰℓ,r\mathcal{E}_{\ell,r}. Its matrix is therefore the range-rr adjacency matrix written in the computational basis indexed by 𝒱ℓ\mathcal{V}_{\ell},

(Aℓ,r)σ​τ=⟨σ|H^r±|τ⟩={1,{σ,τ}∈ℰℓ,r0,otherwise.\left(A_{\ell,r}\right)_{\sigma\tau}=\braket{\sigma|\hat{H}_{r}^{\pm}|\tau}=\begin{cases}1,\quad\{\sigma,\tau\}\in\mathcal{E}_{\ell,r}\\ 0,\quad\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} (14)

The full unweighted adjacency matrix is

Aℓ=∑r=12Aℓ,rA_{\ell}=\sum_{r=1}^{2}A_{\ell,r} (15)

Assign weight Jr/2J_{r}/2 to each range-rr HG edge. The resulting coupling-weighted adjacency matrix is

Wℓ=∑r=12Wℓ,r,Wℓ,r=Jr2​Aℓ,rW_{\ell}=\sum_{r=1}^{2}W_{\ell,r}\,,\quad W_{\ell,r}=\frac{J_{r}}{2}\,A_{\ell,r} (16)

The degree matrix of a graph gives us the number of connections each vertex has. For the unweighted adjacency matrix of the HG, the degree matrix is determined by the number of antiparallel bonds. For a configuration σ∈𝒱ℓ\sigma\in\mathcal{V}_{\ell}, let

nrap​(σ)=|{{i,j}∈Er:σ(i)≠σ(j)}|n_{r}^{\mathrm{ap}}(\sigma)=\left|\left\{\{i,j\}\in E_{r}:\sigma^{(i)}\neq\sigma^{(j)}\right\}\right| (17)

be the number of antiparallel range-rr bonds. Each such bond supports one range-rr HF, so nrap​(σ)n_{r}^{\mathrm{ap}}(\sigma) is the unweighted range-rr degree of σ\sigma. The coupling-weighted degree matrix is therefore

(Dℓ)σ​σ=12​∑r=12Jr​nrap​(σ)=∑τ∈𝒱ℓ(Wℓ)σ​τ.(D_{\ell})_{\sigma\sigma}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{r=1}^{2}J_{r}n_{r}^{\rm ap}(\sigma)=\sum_{\tau\in\mathcal{V}_{\ell}}(W_{\ell})_{\sigma\tau}. (18)

Since S^iz​S^jz\hat{S}_{i}^{z}\hat{S}_{j}^{z} has eigenvalue 1/41/4 for parallel spins and −1/4-1/4 for antiparallel spins, each antiparallel range-rr bond lowers the Ising energy by Jr/2J_{r}/2 below the ferromagnetic reference energy, and

⟨σ|H^c|σ⟩=EF−(Dℓ)σ​σ,EF=14​∑r=12Jr​|Er|.\braket{\sigma|\hat{H}_{c}|\sigma}=E_{F}-(D_{\ell})_{\sigma\sigma},\qquad E_{F}=\frac{1}{4}\sum_{r=1}^{2}J_{r}|E_{r}|. (19)

In the computational basis indexed by 𝒱ℓ\mathcal{V}_{\ell}, Eq. (19) and the definition of WℓW_{\ell} give us the diagonal (classical) and the off-diagonal (quantum) parts of the Hamiltonian in sector ℓ\ell.

Hℓ,c=EF​I−Dℓ,Hℓ,q=Wℓ.H_{\ell,c}=E_{F}I-D_{\ell},\qquad H_{\ell,q}=W_{\ell}. (20)

Thus, up to the constant shift EFE_{F}, the classical part gives −Dℓ-D_{\ell}, while the quantum part gives the weighted adjacency matrix WℓW_{\ell}. The matrix representation of the Hamiltonian can then be written as

Hℓ=EF​I−Dℓ+Wℓ.H_{\ell}=E_{F}I-D_{\ell}+W_{\ell}. (21)

Defining the coupling-weighted Laplacian of the HG as

Lℓ=Dℓ−Wℓ,L_{\ell}=D_{\ell}-W_{\ell}, (22)

and combining Eqs. (21) with (22) gives

Hℓ=EF​I−Lℓ.H_{\ell}=E_{F}I-L_{\ell}. (23)

After shifting the energy origin by the constant EFE_{F}, we write

Hℓ≡−Lℓ.H_{\ell}\equiv-L_{\ell}. (24)

The identity (24) connects the HAF Hamiltonian to the Laplacian of the HG. It therefore turns the GS problem into a spectral problem on the HG: in each sector, the GS energy of the shifted Hamiltonian is the negative of the largest Laplacian eigenvalue, and the GS is the corresponding Laplacian eigenvector. We order its eigenvalues as

0=λ0≤λ1≤⋯≤λ|𝒱ℓ|−1.0=\lambda_{0}\leq\lambda_{1}\leq\cdots\leq\lambda_{|\mathcal{V}_{\ell}|-1}.

Eq. (24) shows that HℓH_{\ell} and LℓL_{\ell} have the same eigenvectors, while their eigenvalues have opposite signs. If the Hamiltonian energies in sector ℓ\ell are ordered as E0≤E1≤⋯≤E|𝒱ℓ|−1E_{0}\leq E_{1}\leq\cdots\leq E_{|\mathcal{V}_{\ell}|-1}, then

Ej=−λ|𝒱ℓ|−1−j,j=0,1,…,|𝒱ℓ|−1.E_{j}=-\lambda_{|\mathcal{V}_{\ell}|-1-j},\qquad j=0,1,\ldots,|\mathcal{V}_{\ell}|-1. (25)

The highest Hamiltonian energy is E|𝒱ℓ|−1=−λ0=0E_{|\mathcal{V}_{\ell}|-1}=-\lambda_{0}=0. The corresponding Laplacian zero mode is the uniform superposition of all configurations in 𝒱ℓ\mathcal{V}_{\ell}. In sector ℓ=0\ell=0, there is only one configuration, the state with all spins down, so this state itself is the zero mode.

For an HG with more than one vertex, the zero eigenvalue is nondegenerate because the HG is connected [19], and the second-smallest Laplacian eigenvalue λ1>0\lambda_{1}>0 is the Fiedler eigenvalue, also called the algebraic connectivity, which measures how well connected the HG is. Since the two spectra are reversed, it fixes the second-highest Hamiltonian energy in sector ℓ\ell,

E|𝒱ℓ|−2=−λ1,E_{|\mathcal{V}_{\ell}|-2}=-\lambda_{1}, (26)

which is negative of the Fiedler value. The GS energy in sector ℓ\ell is the negative of the largest Laplacian eigenvalue,

E0=−λ|𝒱ℓ|−1.E_{0}=-\lambda_{|\mathcal{V}_{\ell}|-1}. (27)

The relation between the Heisenberg Hamiltonian and graph Laplacians in Eq. (24) appeared in different contexts [49, 50, 3]. Theorem 1 below states the correspondence for coupling-weighted HGs. For the J1J_{1}–J2J_{2} HAF, LℓL_{\ell} separates into its NN and NNN contributions.

Theorem 1 (Hilbert–Token Graph Correspondence).

Let G=(V,E)G=(V,E) be a finite, simple, undirected graph whose edge set is partitioned into disjoint bond sets,

E=⨆rEr,E=\bigsqcup_{r}E_{r},

as determined by the lattice geometry. For each ErE_{r}, let Jr>0J_{r}>0 denote the corresponding antiferromagnetic coupling. The HAF Hamiltonian on GG is

H^=∑rJr​∑{i,j}∈Er𝐒^i⋅𝐒^j.\hat{H}=\sum_{r}J_{r}\sum_{\{i,j\}\in E_{r}}\hat{\mathbf{S}}_{i}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{S}}_{j}.

Fix a sector ℓ∈{0,1,…,N}\ell\in\{0,1,\ldots,N\}. Then:

  1. (i)

    As an unweighted graph, the HG in sector ℓ\ell is isomorphic to the ℓ\ell token graph of GG,

    Γℓ​(G)≅Fℓ​(G).\Gamma_{\ell}(G)\cong F_{\ell}(G). (28)

    Here Γℓ​(G)\Gamma_{\ell}(G) is the HG defined in Eq. (9).

  2. (ii)

    In the computational basis indexed by 𝒱ℓ\mathcal{V}_{\ell}, the Hamiltonian matrix HℓH_{\ell}, after subtracting the ferromagnetic reference energy, satisfies

    Hℓ=−Lℓ.H_{\ell}=-L_{\ell}. (29)

    Here Lℓ=Dℓ−WℓL_{\ell}=D_{\ell}-W_{\ell} is the coupling-weighted HG Laplacian of Eq. (22), which decomposes as

    Lℓ=∑rJr2​Lℓ,r,Lℓ,r=Dℓ,r−Aℓ,r,L_{\ell}=\sum_{r}\frac{J_{r}}{2}\,L_{\ell,r},\qquad L_{\ell,r}=D_{\ell,r}-A_{\ell,r}, (30)

    where Dℓ,rD_{\ell,r} and Aℓ,rA_{\ell,r} are the unweighted range-rr degree and adjacency matrices.

  3. (iii)

    After the same energy shift, the spectrum of HℓH_{\ell} is the negative of the Laplacian spectrum,

    spec⁡(Hℓ)=−spec⁡(Lℓ).\operatorname{spec}(H_{\ell})=-\operatorname{spec}(L_{\ell}). (31)

    In particular, the GS energy in sector ℓ\ell is the negative of the largest eigenvalue of the graph Laplacian.

    Emin​(Hℓ)=−λmax​(Lℓ).E_{\min}(H_{\ell})=-\lambda_{\max}(L_{\ell}). (32)
Proof.

Part (i) follows directly from the TG identification in Eq. (13).

For part (ii), Eqs. (3) and (16) show that the exchange part of the Hamiltonian gives the weighted HG adjacency operator. Eq. (20) gives the diagonal contribution as the HG degree operator, together with the ferromagnetic reference energy. Using the definition of the weighted HG Laplacian in Eq. (22), and subtracting the reference energy, gives Hℓ=−LℓH_{\ell}=-L_{\ell}.

The decomposition in Eq. (30) follows by collecting the contributions from each bond set ErE_{r}. This proves part (ii).

Part (iii) follows from part (ii). Multiplication by −1-1 preserves the eigenvectors and reverses the signs and ordering of the eigenvalues. Therefore,

spec⁡(Hℓ)=−spec⁡(Lℓ).\operatorname{spec}(H_{\ell})=-\operatorname{spec}(L_{\ell}).

The smallest eigenvalue of HℓH_{\ell} corresponds to the largest eigenvalue of LℓL_{\ell}, giving Eq. (32). ∎

Theorem 1 underlies our later study of the sign structure of the variational wavefunction and of the stoquasticity of the HAF Hamiltonian. For now we will use it with the S​U​(2)SU(2) symmetry of the Heisenberg Hamiltonian, to show how a property of token graph Laplacian spectrum is connected to the GS for even NN living in the zero-magnetization sector.

II.3 Laplacian Spectrum and GS Magnetization

We have shown that the largest eigenvalue of the graph Laplacian corresponds to the GS energy. In this section, we determine the magnetization sector of the GS. Lieb and Mattis [36] showed that, for an even number of sites, the HAF GS on a bipartite lattice lies in the zero-magnetization sector. Here we show that this also holds for non-bipartite geometries by combining angular-momentum algebra with the spectral inclusion result for token-graph Laplacians [16].

We consider an isotropic Heisenberg model on the physical graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E), with bond-dependent couplings Ji​jJ_{ij}.

H¯^=∑{i,j}∈EJi​j​𝐒^i⋅𝐒^j,Ji​j∈ℝ\hat{\bar{H}}=\sum_{\{i,j\}\in E}J_{ij}\,\mathbf{\hat{S}}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{\hat{S}}_{j},\quad J_{ij}\in\mathbb{R} (33)

Using the notation of HF used in Eq. (4), this Hamiltonian generates the weighted adjacency matrix,

(W¯ℓ)σ​τ={Ji​j/2,σ​⇌i​j​τ​ and ​{i,j}∈E,0,otherwise,(\bar{W}_{\ell})_{\sigma\tau}=\begin{cases}J_{ij}/2,&\sigma\overset{ij}{\rightleftharpoons}\tau\text{ and }\{i,j\}\in E,\\ 0,&\text{otherwise,}\end{cases}

for sector ℓ\ell spin configurations σ,τ∈𝒱ℓ\sigma,\tau\in\mathcal{V}_{\ell}. Now, we can think of the couplings Ji​jJ_{ij} as weights on the physical graph GG. Then the token graph inherits these weights through HF. In the language of Ref. [19], if the symmetric difference between two token graph vertices connected by an edge is {i,j}\{i,j\}, then that edge inherits the parent graph weight Ji​jJ_{ij} (scaled by a factor of 1/21/2). The Laplacian of this weighted token graph, L¯ℓ\bar{L}_{\ell}, is connected to the matrix representation of the Hamiltonian in sector ℓ\ell, H¯ℓ\bar{H}_{\ell} as

H¯ℓ=E¯F​I−L¯ℓ,E¯F=∑{i,j}∈EJi​j4\bar{H}_{\ell}=\bar{E}_{F}\,I-\bar{L}_{\ell},\qquad\bar{E}_{F}=\sum_{\{i,j\}\in E}\frac{J_{ij}}{4} (34)

The Heisenberg Hamiltonian is S​U​(2)SU(2) symmetric. Thus, we can find a simultaneous orthonormal eigenbasis of H¯^\hat{\bar{H}}, 𝐒tot2\mathbf{S}^{2}_{\mathrm{tot}}, and StotzS^{z}_{\mathrm{tot}}, as they are mutually commuting operators. Then, the energy eigenstates are also angular momentum eigenstates labeled as |E,s,ms⟩\ket{E,s,m_{s}}, where EE, s⁡(s+1)s(s+1), and msm_{s} are the eigenvalues of H¯^\hat{\bar{H}}, 𝐒tot2\mathbf{S}^{2}_{\mathrm{tot}}, and StotzS^{z}_{\mathrm{tot}}, respectively. Each eigenstate belongs to the ℓ=ms+N/2\ell=m_{s}+N/2 sector (5) and can be expressed as a superposition of basis states in 𝒱ℓ\mathcal{V}_{\ell}, making it an eigenvector of H¯ℓ\bar{H}_{\ell}. The ladder operators Stot±S^{\pm}_{\mathrm{tot}} commute with the Hamiltonian; hence, applying them to the eigenstates generates states with the same energy and spin but different magnetization. In other words, the ladder operators move the eigenstates from one sector to another

Stot±​|E,s,ms⟩≡|E,s,ms±1⟩,|ms±1|≤s.S^{\pm}_{\mathrm{tot}}\ket{E,s,m_{s}}\equiv\ket{E,s,m_{s}\pm 1},\qquad|m_{s}\pm 1|\leq s.

All eigenstates in a single multiplet have the same energy; therefore, an eigenstate with spin ss has degeneracy at least 2​s+12s+1.

Theorem 2 (Nested Spectrum).

The spectrum of H¯ℓ\bar{H}_{\ell} is nested such that the sector closer to zero magnetization contains the spectra of sectors farther away.

spec⁡(H¯ℓ)⊆spec⁡(H¯ℓ+1),\displaystyle\mathrm{spec}(\bar{H}_{\ell})\subseteq\mathrm{spec}(\bar{H}_{\ell+1}), 1≤ℓ<N/2,\displaystyle 1\leq\ell<N/2,
spec⁡(H¯ℓ)⊇spec⁡(H¯ℓ+1),\displaystyle\mathrm{spec}(\bar{H}_{\ell})\supseteq\mathrm{spec}(\bar{H}_{\ell+1}), N/2≤ℓ≤N.\displaystyle N/2\leq\ell\leq N.
Proof.

Assume we are in sector ℓ\ell. Since ms=ℓ−N/2m_{s}=\ell-N/2 every eigenvector, |E,s,ms⟩\ket{E,s,m_{s}}, of H¯ℓ\bar{H}_{\ell} has spin s≥|ℓ−N/2|s\geq|\ell-N/2|. For 1≤ℓ<N/21\leq\ell<N/2, we can use Stot+S^{+}_{\mathrm{tot}} to move all the eigenvectors to the sector ℓ+1\ell+1. These eigenvectors have the same energy eigenvalues in sector ℓ+1\ell+1 as in sector ℓ\ell, since the ladder operators commute with the Hamiltonian. For ℓ≥N/2\ell\geq N/2 the same arguments using Stot−S^{-}_{\mathrm{tot}} lead to spec⁡(H¯ℓ+1)⊆spec⁡(H¯ℓ)\mathrm{spec}(\bar{H}_{\ell+1})\subseteq\mathrm{spec}(\bar{H}_{\ell}). ∎

Corollary 1 (GS Magnetization).

The GS of H¯⌊N/2⌋\bar{H}_{\lfloor N/2\rfloor} corresponds to the GS of H¯^\hat{\bar{H}}, in other words, the ℓ=⌊N/2⌋\ell=\lfloor N/2\rfloor sector contains a GS of H¯^\hat{\bar{H}}. For an even number of spins, this is the zero magnetization sector.

Proof.

The corollary follows directly from Theorem 2 since spec⁡(H¯⌊N/2⌋)\mathrm{spec}(\bar{H}_{\lfloor N/2\rfloor}) contains the spectra of all other sectors. No matter the magnetization of GS, we can always bring it to ⌊N/2⌋\lfloor N/2\rfloor sector by repeated application of a ladder operator without changing energy eigenvalue. The choice of ℓ=⌊N/2⌋\ell=\lfloor N/2\rfloor is not unique, the ℓ=⌈N/2⌉\ell=\lceil N/2\rceil sector works just as well for odd number of spins due to duality (12). ∎

Since the Hamiltonian and the Laplacian are related by Eq. (34), spec⁡(L¯ℓ)⊆spec⁡(L¯ℓ+1)\mathrm{spec}(\bar{L}_{\ell})\subseteq\mathrm{spec}(\bar{L}_{\ell+1}) for 1≤ℓ<N/21\leq\ell<N/2. This theorem was proven in Ref. [16] for the unweighted case, i.e., Ji​j=2J_{ij}=2, and was extended to the weighted case in Ref. [3]. However, neither work used the S​U​(2)SU(2) invariance to prove this result. Our approach shows a physical reason for why the nested spectrum property is true, that it is a consequence of the S​U​(2)SU(2) symmetry and angular momentum eigenstates, and thus provides an example of how purely quantum mechanical approach can be used to study the token graph Laplacian.

Theorem 2 makes no claim about whether there exists a singlet GS or if all GS are singlet, for even number of spins. All GS being singlet is equivalent to the following strict inequality in token graph language.

λmax​(L¯N/2−1)<λmax​(L¯N/2)\lambda_{\mathrm{max}}(\bar{L}_{N/2-1})<\lambda_{\mathrm{max}}(\bar{L}_{N/2})

According to Lieb and Mattis [36], this is true for connected bipartite graphs with antiferromagnetic couplings, when the bipartition divides the graph into two parts with equal number of vertices. However, no analytical proof exists for commonly used non-bipartite graphs, such as the periodic square lattice with NN and NNN edges for J2/J1>0.5J_{2}/J_{1}>0.5 (The J2/J1≤0.5J_{2}/J_{1}\leq 0.5 case was proven by Tanaka [67]). We believe insights from token graph literature can help address this analytically.

III Structure of the Hilbert graph

We now use the definition of the HG and its adjacency matrices in Eqs. (14) and (15) to study HG properties relevant to our work: bipartiteness, triangle count, and the Estrada bipartivity index [18]. The first provides a structural condition, while the latter two characterize odd cycles in HG.

III.1 Bipartiteness Inheritance

The HG inherits both bipartiteness and odd cycles from the parent interaction graph GG; a bipartition of GG yields a two-coloring of Γℓ​(G)\Gamma_{\ell}(G), and an odd cycle in GG yields an odd cycle in the HG. The following theorems prove these two inheritance properties.

Theorem 3 (Cycle inheritance).

Let G=(V,E)G=(V,E) be a finite simple undirected graph and 1≤ℓ≤|V|−11\leq\ell\leq|V|-1. Then, any cycle in GG can be mapped to a cycle of the same length in Γℓ​(G)\Gamma_{\ell}(G).

Proof.

Consider a cycle i1,i2,…,iLi_{1},i_{2},\ldots,i_{L} in GG, where iki_{k} are unique vertices of GG. First we assume L≤ℓ+1L\leq\ell+1 and place a down spin at i1i_{1} and up spin on the rest of the cycle. The remaining vertices are always assumed to be filled in a way that satisfies the magnetization sector. Using HF we can transfer the down spin at i1i_{1} as i1→i2→…→iL→i1i_{1}\to i_{2}\to\ldots\to i_{L}\to i_{1}, which creates a cycle in Γℓ​(G)\Gamma_{\ell}(G) of length LL. Now we consider L>ℓ+1L>\ell+1 and fill i1,i2,…,iℓi_{1},i_{2},\ldots,i_{\ell} with up spins and iℓ+1,…,iLi_{\ell+1},\ldots,i_{L} with down spins. We move the up spin at iℓi_{\ell} as iℓ→iℓ+1→…→iLi_{\ell}\to i_{\ell+1}\to\ldots\to i_{L}, taking L−ℓL-\ell HFs. We then move the up spins at i1,i2,…,iℓ−1i_{1},i_{2},\ldots,i_{\ell-1} as ik→ik+1i_{k}\to i_{k+1} starting from iℓ−1i_{\ell-1} and stopping at i1i_{1}. This takes another ℓ−1\ell-1 HFs. Now we have a down spin at i1i_{1} and an up spin at iLi_{L}, which we exchange using another HF. This creates a cycle of length (L−ℓ)+(ℓ−1)+1=L(L-\ell)+(\ell-1)+1=L in Γℓ​(G)\Gamma_{\ell}(G). ∎

The theorem above shows that any odd cycles in GG yield odd cycles in Γℓ​(G)\Gamma_{\ell}(G). It follows that if GG is non-bipartite, Γℓ​(G)\Gamma_{\ell}(G) must also be non-bipartite. Nevertheless, this construction does not account for all the odd cycles in the HG; in general, the HG may have additional odd cycles which are not direct images of cycles of the same length in GG. The next theorem, which was first proved in [19], states that if GG contains no odd cycles, then Γℓ​(G)\Gamma_{\ell}(G) cannot have any odd cycles.

Theorem 4 (Bipartiteness inheritance).

Let G=(V,E)G=(V,E) be a finite simple undirected graph. For 1≤ℓ≤|V|−11\leq\ell\leq|V|-1, Γℓ​(G)\Gamma_{\ell}(G) is bipartite if and only if GG is bipartite.

Proof.

Theorem 3 shows that if GG is non-bipartite then so is Γℓ​(G)\Gamma_{\ell}(G). Now we only need to show that if GG is bipartite then so is Γℓ​(G)\Gamma_{\ell}(G). Suppose GG is bipartite. Then its vertex set is a union of two non-empty disjoint sets, or sublattices, V=VA⊔VBV=V_{A}\sqcup V_{B}, such that every edge of GG has one endpoint in VAV_{A} and the other in VBV_{B}. For a configuration σ∈𝒱ℓ\sigma\in\mathcal{V}_{\ell} define the number of up spins in VAV_{A} as

NA↑​(σ):=|{i∈VA:σ(i)=↑}|,N_{A}^{\uparrow}(\sigma):=\lvert\{i\in V_{A}:\sigma^{(i)}=\,\uparrow\}\rvert, (35)

and its parity

Π⁡(σ):=(−1)NA↑​(σ).\Pi(\sigma):=(-1)^{N_{A}^{\uparrow}(\sigma)}. (36)

Let {σ,τ}∈ℰℓ\{\sigma,\tau\}\in\mathcal{E}_{\ell} be an HG edge. Then τ\tau is obtained from σ\sigma by an HF on some bond {i,j}∈E\{i,j\}\in E, with i∈VAi\in V_{A} and j∈VBj\in V_{B}. For an HF, the two spins on this bond are antiparallel, meaning only one spin is up. After the flip, the up spin moves from either VAV_{A} to VBV_{B} or VBV_{B} to VAV_{A}. Hence NA↑N_{A}^{\uparrow} changes by ±1\pm 1, and therefore

Π⁡(τ)=−Π⁡(σ)\Pi(\tau)=-\Pi(\sigma)

on every HG edge. Thus, Π\Pi gives a two-coloring of Γℓ​(G)\Gamma_{\ell}(G), making it bipartite. ∎

The parity Π⁡(σ)=(−1)NA↑​(σ)\Pi(\sigma)=(-1)^{N_{A}^{\uparrow}(\sigma)} is the well-known MSR, which follows from Theorem 4. Thus, when the physical graph GG is bipartite, the MSR assigns signs to the HG vertices that define its bipartition. Same-sublattice couplings, such as J2J_{2} bonds on the square lattice, connect HG vertices with the same Π⁡(σ)\Pi(\sigma) value, so this coloring is no longer proper.

The non-bipartiteness therefore manifests in the HG through triangles and higher-order odd cycles. We next count triangles in the HG.

III.2 Triangle Count

The shortest odd cycles in the HG are triangles, which we read from the unweighted adjacency matrix AℓA_{\ell} in Eq. (15). Since (Aℓ3)σ​σ\left(A_{\ell}^{3}\right)_{\sigma\sigma} counts closed walks of length three based at σ\sigma, each triangle contributes six closed walks of length three: three starting vertices and two traversal directions. The number of triangles in the HG is therefore [73]

N△​(Γℓ)=16​Tr⁡(Aℓ3).N_{\triangle}(\Gamma_{\ell})=\frac{1}{6}\,\operatorname{Tr}\!\left(A_{\ell}^{3}\right). (37)

A positive value of N△​(Γℓ)N_{\triangle}(\Gamma_{\ell}) certifies that the HG contains triangles and is therefore not bipartite; by Theorem 4, this can occur only when the physical lattice GG is itself non-bipartite.

In Table 1, we show N△N_{\triangle}, computed from AℓA_{\ell} using Eq. (37), for the J1J_{1}–J2J_{2} chain, square, and triangular-lattice HGs under periodic and open boundary conditions in the zero-magnetization sector at N=16N=16.

We note that in the chain and square lattice cases, the HG contains no triangles when J2=0J_{2}=0. This is consistent with Theorem 4, showing that if the parent graph is bipartite, its HG is as well. In the triangular lattice, however, the HG contains triangles when J2=0J_{2}=0. This shows that the HG inherits triangles from its parent graph. For non-zero J2J_{2}, all three HGs inherit triangles from their respective parent graph.

We later show that the signs of the variational wavefunction, or equivalently the signs of the off-diagonal part of the HAF Hamiltonian, define an antiferromagnetic Ising model on the HG. For non-bipartite geometries, these triangles are the origin of geometric frustration in the HG, which prevents a Marshall-type phase prior for the wavefunction. Triangles on the HG can be sufficient to create geometric frustration, but not necessary. Following Theorem 3, an HG may contain higher-order odd cycles.

The triangle count provides a one-sided witness: N△>0N_{\triangle}>0 proves that the HG is non-bipartite, whereas N△=0N_{\triangle}=0 does not prove the bipartiteness. In the next section, we show that the Estrada bipartivity index accounts for these higher-order odd cycles.

III.3 Estrada Bipartivity Index

The Estrada bipartivity index [18] is a spectral measure based on the weighted proportion of even closed walks to all closed walks in a graph. It equals one for a bipartite graph, where every closed walk has even length, and falls below one when odd closed walks are present.

The number of walks from σ\sigma to τ\tau of length kk in Γℓ\Gamma_{\ell} is equal to (Aℓk)σ​τ(A_{\ell}^{k})_{\sigma\tau}. Therefore, Tr⁡(Aℓk)=∑σ∈𝒱ℓ(Aℓk)σ​σ\operatorname{Tr}(A^{k}_{\ell})=\sum_{\sigma\in\mathcal{V}_{\ell}}(A^{k}_{\ell})_{\sigma\sigma} gives us the total number of closed walks of length kk. However, this number can diverge as kk gets larger. Estrada and Rodríguez-Velázquez [18] used a factor of 1/k!1/k! which accounts for this divergence. Then, a measure of all even closed walks is

Tr⁡cosh⁡Aℓ=∑k=0∞1(2​k)!​Tr⁡(Aℓ2​k)\operatorname{Tr}\cosh A_{\ell}=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{(2k)!}\operatorname{Tr}(A^{2k}_{\ell})

and a measure of all odd closed walks is,

Tr⁡sinh⁡Aℓ=∑k=0∞1(2​k+1)!​Tr⁡(Aℓ2​k+1).\operatorname{Tr}\sinh A_{\ell}=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{(2k+1)!}\operatorname{Tr}(A^{2k+1}_{\ell}).

Since Tr⁡(Aℓ)=0\operatorname{Tr}(A_{\ell})=0 by definition, the first, or leading, term in the expansion of Tr⁡sinh⁡Aℓ\operatorname{Tr}\sinh A_{\ell} is N△N_{\triangle} (37). The contributions from higher-order odd closed walks are also included, but with smaller weight factors. Now, the Estrada bipartivity is defined as the proportion of even to total closed walks.

β⁡(Γℓ)=Tr⁡cosh⁡AℓTr⁡cosh⁡Aℓ+Tr⁡sinh⁡Aℓ=Tr⁡cosh⁡AℓTr⁡eAℓ\beta(\Gamma_{\ell})=\frac{\operatorname{Tr}\cosh A_{\ell}}{\operatorname{Tr}\cosh A_{\ell}+\operatorname{Tr}\sinh A_{\ell}}=\frac{\operatorname{Tr}\cosh A_{\ell}}{\operatorname{Tr}\,e^{A_{\ell}}}

In terms of eigenvalues of AℓA_{\ell}, denoted by {λi}\{\lambda_{i}\} we can express the bipartivity as,

β⁡(Γℓ)=∑icosh⁡λi∑ieλi\beta(\Gamma_{\ell})=\frac{\sum_{i}\cosh\lambda_{i}}{\sum_{i}e^{\lambda_{i}}} (38)

Unlike the triangle count, β\beta includes closed walks of every length. It satisfies [18]

12<β⁡(Γℓ)≤1.\tfrac{1}{2}<\beta(\Gamma_{\ell})\leq 1. (39)

The upper bound β=1\beta=1 is attained when all the closed walks are even, and the contribution from odd closed walks is zero, i.e., Tr⁡sinh⁡Aℓ=0\operatorname{Tr}\sinh A_{\ell}=0. This can only happen when Tr⁡(Aℓ2​k+1)=0​∀k\operatorname{Tr}(A_{\ell}^{2k+1})=0\ \forall k, meaning there are no odd closed walks in the graph. Therefore, β​(Γℓ​(G))=1\beta(\Gamma_{\ell}(G))=1 implies Γℓ​(G)\Gamma_{\ell}(G) is bipartite and by Theorem 4 it also implies that GG is bipartite. Conversely, any value below unity signals at least one odd closed walk, so no global two-coloring of Γℓ​(G)\Gamma_{\ell}(G) exists.

Table 1 shows β\beta for the zero-magnetization HGs of the J1J_{1}–J2J_{2} HAF on the chain, square, and triangular lattices. At J2=0J_{2}=0, the chain and square HGs are bipartite and have β=1\beta=1, whereas the triangular lattice HG is non-bipartite and has β≃0.50\beta\simeq 0.50. For nonzero J2J_{2}, β\beta drops to 0.510.51 for the chain and to approximately 0.500.50 for the square, while remaining near 0.500.50 for the triangular lattice. To the precision shown, these values are unchanged between periodic and open boundary conditions.

In the next section, we write the HAF energy directly as a functional on the HG in a fixed-magnetization sector. This form shows how the HG topology constrains phase reconstruction of a variational wavefunction and connects it to Max-Cut.

IV The Energy Functional and Max-Cut

In this section we study the eigenvalue problem associated with the identity in Eq. (23), first from the combinatorial side. We show that Max-Cut on the HG, relaxed from the sign variables to the unit sphere, becomes the eigenvalue problem for the Laplacian, so that computing the GS energy is solving a spectrally relaxed Max-Cut instance. This also shows the origin of the edgewise antiferromagnetic condition. We then look at the same problem from the side of the Hamiltonian and its GS, and identify the optimal sign structure of the variational wavefunction as the manifestation of that condition. Finally, at fixed amplitudes, we study the complexity of phase reconstruction.

IV.1 Spectral Relaxation of HG Max-Cut

Equation (23) Hℓ=EF−LℓH_{\ell}=E_{F}-L_{\ell} says that the GS of HℓH_{\ell} is the eigenvector of LℓL_{\ell} with the largest eigenvalue,

Eℓ,0=EF−λmax​(Lℓ).E_{\ell,0}=E_{F}-\lambda_{\mathrm{max}}(L_{\ell}).

Since Lℓ=Dℓ−WℓL_{\ell}=D_{\ell}-W_{\ell}, with each diagonal entry of DℓD_{\ell} equal to the sum of the weights in the corresponding row of WℓW_{\ell}, the expectation value of LℓL_{\ell} for a real vector |x⟩|x\rangle with components xσ=⟨σ|x⟩x_{\sigma}=\langle\sigma|x\rangle is a sum over HG edges. Expanding |x⟩|x\rangle in the orthonormal eigenbasis of the real symmetric matrix LℓL_{\ell} bounds it from above:

⟨x|Lℓ|x⟩⟨x|x⟩=∑{σ,τ}∈ℰℓ(Wℓ)σ​τ​(xσ−xτ)2⟨x|x⟩≤λmax​(Lℓ).\frac{\braket{x|L_{\ell}|x}}{\braket{x|x}}=\sum_{\{\sigma,\tau\}\in\mathcal{E}_{\ell}}(W_{\ell})_{\sigma\tau}\frac{(x_{\sigma}-x_{\tau})^{2}}{\braket{x|x}}\leq\lambda_{\mathrm{max}}(L_{\ell}). (40)

Here, we used the fact that each row of the Laplacian LℓL_{\ell} sums to zero. This inequality is the variational principle expressed in terms of the graph Laplacian, and equality holds only when |x⟩\ket{x} is the largest eigenvector of the Laplacian. Additionally, this inequality tells us that the GS is the real vector whose components vary as strongly as possible across HFs, in the weighted quadratic sense of Eq. (40) at fixed norm. We immediately see that to maximize ⟨x|Lℓ|x⟩\braket{x|L_{\ell}|x}, we should prioritize opposite signs for xσx_{\sigma} and xτx_{\tau}, since this increases (xσ−xτ)2(x_{\sigma}-x_{\tau})^{2}. In other words, we must try to satisfy the condition,

sign⁡(xσ)​sign​(xτ)=−1,\mathrm{sign}(x_{\sigma})\ \mathrm{sign}(x_{\tau})=-1, (41)

for as many edges in HG as possible. Setting this condition for all edges is possible if and only if Γℓ\Gamma_{\ell} is bipartite. In the presence of frustration or odd cycles, we cannot satisfy this condition for all edges, and in that case we have to prioritize some edges over others depending on the values of the weights and values of |xσ|,|xτ||x_{\sigma}|,\,|x_{\tau}|. This is the origin of PRP for GS. The frustration in the sign structure of the GS is directly induced by the odd cycles in HG. Theorem 4 states that odd cycles in HG directly follow from odd cycles in the physical graph. Thus, the physical graph topology dictates the frustration in the GS sign structure, and choosing the optimal sign structure becomes a combinatorial optimization problem over HG. In fact, this relates to Max-Cut on HG, as we show in the current section and the next.

In a graph, an edge is said to be cut when the two vertices end up on different sides of the cut. We use sign⁡(xσ)\mathrm{sign}(x_{\sigma}) to show which side of the cut the vertex σ\sigma is on. Hence, the edge {σ,τ}\{\sigma,\tau\} is a cut edge if xσx_{\sigma} and xτx_{\tau} have opposite signs; otherwise, the edge is not cut. A weight (Wℓ)σ​τ(W_{\ell})_{\sigma\tau} is associated with each edge. The weighted cut value, determined by the sign pattern of the vector |x⟩\ket{x}, is the sum of the weights of all cut edges.

CutWℓ​(x)=∑{σ,τ}∈ℰℓ(Wℓ)σ​τ​1−sign⁡(xσ)​sign​(xτ)2.\mathrm{Cut}_{W_{\ell}}(x)=\sum_{\{\sigma,\tau\}\in\mathcal{E}_{\ell}}(W_{\ell})_{\sigma\tau}\,\frac{1-\mathrm{sign}(x_{\sigma})\,\mathrm{sign}(x_{\tau})}{2}. (42)

Restricting to binary values, xσ=±1x_{\sigma}=\pm 1, then (xσ−xτ)2=2​(1−xσ​xτ)(x_{\sigma}-x_{\tau})^{2}=2\,(1-x_{\sigma}x_{\tau}) and the cut value can be written in terms of the expectation of the Laplacian

CutWℓ​(x)=14​⟨x|Lℓ|x⟩;|x⟩∈{±1}|𝒱ℓ|.\mathrm{Cut}_{W_{\ell}}(x)=\frac{1}{4}\,\braket{x|L_{\ell}|x};\quad\ket{x}\in\{\pm 1\}^{|\mathcal{V}_{\ell}|}.

Geometrically, this restriction to binary values means we choose points from the vertices of a Boolean hypercube, as shown in Fig. 2. Now, let 𝒞ℓ\mathcal{C}_{\ell} denote the vertex set of the Boolean hypercube, and let 𝒮ℓ\mathcal{S}_{\ell} denote the relaxation of the cube to the hypersphere of radius |𝒱ℓ|\sqrt{|\mathcal{V}_{\ell}|}

𝒮ℓ\displaystyle\mathcal{S}_{\ell} ={|x⟩∈ℝ|𝒱ℓ|:⟨x|x⟩=|𝒱ℓ|}\displaystyle=\{\ket{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{V}_{\ell}|}:\braket{x|x}=|\mathcal{V}_{\ell}|\}
𝒞ℓ\displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{\ell} ={|x⟩∈𝒮ℓ:xσ=±1}.\displaystyle=\{\ket{x}\in\mathcal{S}_{\ell}:x_{\sigma}=\pm 1\}.

Then, determining the Max-Cut value and the maximum eigenvalue of the Laplacian becomes the following objectives over these sets

Max-Cut​(Wℓ)\displaystyle\textsf{Max-Cut}(W_{\ell}) =max|x⟩∈𝒞ℓ⁡14​⟨x|Lℓ|x⟩\displaystyle=\max_{\ket{x}\in\mathcal{C}_{\ell}}\frac{1}{4}\,\braket{x|L_{\ell}|x}
λmax​(Lℓ)\displaystyle\lambda_{\mathrm{max}}(L_{\ell}) =max|x⟩∈𝒮ℓ⁡1|𝒱ℓ|​⟨x|Lℓ|x⟩.\displaystyle=\max_{\ket{x}\in\mathcal{S}_{\ell}}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{V}_{\ell}|}\,\braket{x|L_{\ell}|x}.

Moreover, we can extend this result to the complex hypersphere because LℓL_{\ell} is Hermitian.

𝒮ℓ⋆\displaystyle\mathcal{S}^{\star}_{\ell} ={|x⟩∈ℂ|𝒱ℓ|:⟨x|x⟩=|𝒱ℓ|}\displaystyle=\{\ket{x}\in\mathbb{C}^{|\mathcal{V}_{\ell}|}:\braket{x|x}=|\mathcal{V}_{\ell}|\}
λmax​(Lℓ)\displaystyle\lambda_{\mathrm{max}}(L_{\ell}) =max|x⟩∈𝒮ℓ⋆⁡1|𝒱ℓ|​⟨x|Lℓ|x⟩.\displaystyle=\max_{\ket{x}\in\mathcal{S}^{\star}_{\ell}}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{V}_{\ell}|}\,\braket{x|L_{\ell}|x}.

These equations connect Max-Cut to the largest eigenvalue of the graph Laplacian [43]. Relaxing the search space of Max-Cut from the vertices of the Boolean hypercube to the corresponding real or complex hypersphere yields the graph Laplacian’s maximum eigenvalue. In other words, searching for the GS of HℓH_{\ell} can be interpreted as the spectral relaxation of Max-Cut on HG, as described in Fig. 2. Using (40) we can get an inequality relation between the discrete optimization (Max-Cut) and its relaxed continuous counterpart (λmax\lambda_{\mathrm{max}}).

Max-Cut​(Wℓ)≤|𝒱ℓ|4​λmax​(Lℓ)\textsf{Max-Cut}(W_{\ell})\leq\frac{|\mathcal{V}_{\ell}|}{4}\,\lambda_{\mathrm{max}}(L_{\ell})

In terms of GS energy,

Eℓ,0≤EF−4|𝒱ℓ|​Max-Cut​(Wℓ).E_{\ell,0}\leq E_{F}-\frac{4}{|\mathcal{V}_{\ell}|}\textsf{Max-Cut}(W_{\ell}).

The spectral relaxation above therefore acts on the bare coupling-weighted HG and allows the vector |x⟩\ket{x} to vary over the full sphere 𝒮ℓ\mathcal{S}_{\ell}, thereby optimizing its component magnitudes and signs simultaneously (Fig. 1). To isolate phase reconstruction, we now resolve each variational coefficient into a positive amplitude and a phase. Once the amplitude profile is fixed, only the phase degrees of freedom, or equivalently the sign degrees of freedom in the real sector, remain, and the bare HG edge weights are dressed by amplitude products. The resulting discrete sign optimization problem is a weighted Max-Cut problem on the same HG, but it is generally not the bare Max-Cut instance considered above.

IV.2 The Phase Reconstruction Problem

We now study how the wavefunction’s sign structure enters the energy minimization. Eq. (41) already showed that the Laplacian favors opposite signs on neighboring HG vertices for its largest eigenvalue. To make this dependence explicit, we separate the wavefunction into its amplitude and phase. We write a variational state in the sector ℓ\ell as

|Ψℓ⟩=∑σ∈𝒱ℓψσ​ei​ϕσ​|σ⟩;ψσ,ϕσ∈ℝ,ψσ≥0\ket{\Psi_{\ell}}=\sum_{\sigma\in\mathcal{V}_{\ell}}\psi_{\sigma}e^{i\phi_{\sigma}}\ket{\sigma};\quad\psi_{\sigma},\phi_{\sigma}\in\mathbb{R},\,\psi_{\sigma}\geq 0 (43)

and the energy associated with this state is

Eℓ=⟨Ψℓ|Hℓ|Ψℓ⟩⟨Ψℓ|Ψℓ⟩,E_{\ell}=\frac{\braket{\Psi_{\ell}|H_{\ell}|\Psi_{\ell}}}{\braket{\Psi_{\ell}|\Psi_{\ell}}},

when the variational state is non-zero. Since no two sectors share any basis states, we can write any variational state in the full computational basis as,

|Ψ⟩=∑ℓ=0N|Ψℓ⟩\ket{\Psi}=\sum_{\ell=0}^{N}\ket{\Psi_{\ell}}

Our focus in this section is the phase reconstruction problem or PRP. We define PRP as solving for the phases ϕσ\phi_{\sigma} such that the energy expectation of the variational state is minimized for given amplitudes ψσ\psi_{\sigma}.

Definition 1 (Phase Reconstruction Problem (PRP)).

Let {|σ⟩}\{\ket{\sigma}\} be an orthonormal basis of the Hilbert space, let H^\hat{H} be the Hamiltonian, and let {ψσ}\{\psi_{\sigma}\} be a fixed set of non-negative amplitudes. The phase reconstruction problem consists of finding the phases ϕσ∈ℝ\phi_{\sigma}\in\mathbb{R} that minimize the variational energy, ⟨Ψ|H^|Ψ⟩\braket{\Psi|\hat{H}|\Psi} for |Ψ⟩=∑σψσ​ei​ϕσ​|σ⟩\ket{\Psi}=\sum_{\sigma}\psi_{\sigma}e^{i\phi_{\sigma}}\ket{\sigma}. Since wavefunctions have U⁡(1)U(1) symmetry, the solution is defined up to a global phase.

For a non-zero state, the energy expectation in the full computational basis reduces to:

E=⟨Ψ|H^|Ψ⟩⟨Ψ|Ψ⟩=∑⟨Ψℓ|Ψℓ⟩≠0⟨Ψℓ|Ψℓ⟩⟨Ψ|Ψ⟩​EℓE=\frac{\braket{\Psi|\hat{H}|\Psi}}{\braket{\Psi|\Psi}}=\sum_{\braket{\Psi_{\ell}|\Psi_{\ell}}\neq 0}\frac{\braket{\Psi_{\ell}|\Psi_{\ell}}}{\braket{\Psi|\Psi}}\,E_{\ell}

Since ⟨Ψℓ|Ψℓ⟩\braket{\Psi_{\ell}|\Psi_{\ell}} are independent of phase, separately minimizing each EℓE_{\ell} will also minimize EE. In other words, solving PRP in each sector separately solves PRP for the entire Hilbert space. Accordingly, our objective now shifts to energy minimization in each sector separately.

The Hamiltonian in each sector separates into classical and quantum parts, Hℓ=Hℓ,c+Hℓ,qH_{\ell}=H_{\ell,c}+H_{\ell,q}, and so does the energy, Eℓ=Eℓ,c+Eℓ,qE_{\ell}=E_{\ell,c}+E_{\ell,q}.

Eℓ,c=⟨Ψℓ|Hℓ,c|Ψℓ⟩⟨Ψℓ|Ψℓ⟩,\displaystyle E_{\ell,c}=\frac{\braket{\Psi_{\ell}|H_{\ell,c}|\Psi_{\ell}}}{\braket{\Psi_{\ell}|\Psi_{\ell}}}, Eℓ,q=⟨Ψℓ|Hℓ,q|Ψℓ⟩⟨Ψℓ|Ψℓ⟩\displaystyle E_{\ell,q}=\frac{\braket{\Psi_{\ell}|H_{\ell,q}|\Psi_{\ell}}}{\braket{\Psi_{\ell}|\Psi_{\ell}}}

The classical part Eℓ,cE_{\ell,c} is diagonal and thus independent of phase. For phase optimization, we therefore only need to pay attention to the quantum part Eℓ,qE_{\ell,q}, which contains interference terms when written as a sum over HG edges.

Eℓ,q=∑{σ,τ}∈ℰℓ(wℓ)σ​τ​cos⁡(ϕσ−ϕτ),(wℓ)σ​τ≥0.E_{\ell,q}=\sum_{\{\sigma,\tau\}\in\mathcal{E}_{\ell}}(w_{\ell})_{\sigma\tau}\,\cos(\phi_{\sigma}-\phi_{\tau}),\quad(w_{\ell})_{\sigma\tau}\geq 0. (44)

Here wℓw_{\ell} is the sector ℓ\ell amplitude-dressed weight matrix.

(wℓ)σ​τ=2​ψσ​ψτ⟨Ψℓ|Ψℓ⟩​(Hℓ,q)σ​τ(w_{\ell})_{\sigma\tau}=\frac{2\,\psi_{\sigma}\psi_{\tau}}{\braket{\Psi_{\ell}|\Psi_{\ell}}}(H_{\ell,q})_{\sigma\tau} (45)

Eq. (44) is an amplitude-weighted antiferromagnetic XY model on the HG, where each edge in HG has an energy (wℓ)σ​τ​cos⁡(ϕσ−ϕτ)(w_{\ell})_{\sigma\tau}\cos(\phi_{\sigma}-\phi_{\tau}) associated with it. For a physical lattice GG and coupling ratio J2/J1J_{2}/J_{1}, the coupling-dressed weights are fixed. However, the amplitude-dressed weights are emergent: the Hamiltonian provides the bare coupling JrJ_{r}, while the variational state dresses each edge by ψσ​ψτ/⟨Ψℓ|Ψℓ⟩\psi_{\sigma}\psi_{\tau}/\braket{\Psi_{\ell}|\Psi_{\ell}}. As the amplitudes vary, the same HG therefore supports a family of amplitude-weighted XY models in each sector.

Since the active edge weights in Eq. (44) are nonnegative, the energy minimization is governed by the interference term cos⁡(ϕσ−ϕτ)\cos(\phi_{\sigma}-\phi_{\tau}). Every edge weight (wℓ)σ​τ(w_{\ell})_{\sigma\tau} is non-negative for antiferromagnetic couplings, i.e. Jr≥0J_{r}\geq 0, and the edge energy is minimized by cos⁡(ϕσ−ϕτ)=−1\cos(\phi_{\sigma}-\phi_{\tau})=-1, which we call the π\pi-edge condition (PEC). The opposite case, cos⁡(ϕσ−ϕτ)=+1\cos(\phi_{\sigma}-\phi_{\tau})=+1, is the zero-edge condition (ZEC).

(PEC)ϕσ−ϕτ\displaystyle\text{(PEC)}\quad\phi_{\sigma}-\phi_{\tau} ≡π(mod2​π),\displaystyle\equiv\pi\pmod{2\pi}, (46)
(ZEC)ϕσ−ϕτ\displaystyle\text{(ZEC)}\quad\phi_{\sigma}-\phi_{\tau} ≡0(mod2​π).\displaystyle\equiv 0\pmod{2\pi}. (47)

Every edge favors PEC as it locally minimizes the energy, and this preference is independent of the amplitudes: the weights set the magnitude of each edge contribution but never its sign. Whether all edges can satisfy PEC simultaneously therefore depends on the HG’s topology.

Now, consider the assignments of phase factor gσ​τ∈U⁡(1)g_{\sigma\tau}\in U(1) to every edge of Γℓ​(G)\Gamma_{\ell}(G) with gσ​τ−1=gτ​σg_{\sigma\tau}^{-1}=g_{\tau\sigma}. A phase field {ϕσ}\{\phi_{\sigma}\} induces such an assignment through

gσ​τ:=ei⁡(ϕσ−ϕτ),g_{\sigma\tau}:=e^{i(\phi_{\sigma}-\phi_{\tau})}, (48)

but not every assignment is of this form. For any closed loop γ=(σ0,σ1,…,σn−1,σn=σ0)\gamma=(\sigma_{0},\sigma_{1},\dots,\sigma_{n-1},\sigma_{n}=\sigma_{0}) in Γℓ​(G)\Gamma_{\ell}(G), the holonomy of the phase field around γ\gamma is

Holγ:=∏k=0n−1gσk​σk+1.\texttt{Hol}_{\gamma}:=\prod_{k=0}^{n-1}g_{\sigma_{k}\sigma_{k+1}}. (49)

It is invariant under gσ​τ→hσ​gσ​τ​hτ−1g_{\sigma\tau}\rightarrow h_{\sigma}g_{\sigma\tau}h_{\tau}^{-1} for arbitrary hσ∈U⁡(1)h_{\sigma}\in U(1), which is the gauge transformation ϕσ↦ϕσ+ασ\phi_{\sigma}\mapsto\phi_{\sigma}+\alpha_{\sigma} with an arbitrary angle ασ\alpha_{\sigma} at each vertex. Since each gσ​τg_{\sigma\tau} is a difference of vertex phases, the product telescopes and Holγ=1\texttt{Hol}_{\gamma}=1 for every closed loop, whatever the phase field. A global PEC, on the other hand, prescribes gσ​τ=−1g_{\sigma\tau}=-1 on every edge, so Holγ=(−1)|γ|\texttt{Hol}_{\gamma}=(-1)^{|\gamma|}. The two requirements are compatible only if every closed walk in Γℓ​(G)\Gamma_{\ell}(G) has even length. This leads us to re-express the two-coloring theorem in the context of PEC on HG.

Corollary 2 (PEC–bipartiteness).

A global {0,π}\{0,\pi\} phase assignment obeying PEC on every edge exists if and only if Γℓ​(G)\Gamma_{\ell}(G) is bipartite.

The forward proof follows directly from the holonomy argument above. Conversely, if Γℓ​(G)\Gamma_{\ell}(G) is bipartite, assigning phases 00 and π\pi to parts yields PEC on every edge. Since each edge contribution to Eℓ,qE_{\ell,q} is bounded below by −(wℓ)σ​τ-(w_{\ell})_{\sigma\tau}, this assignment saturates the lower bound on every edge simultaneously and therefore gives

Eℓ,q=−∑{σ,τ}∈ℰℓ(wℓ)σ​τ.E_{\ell,q}=-\sum_{\{\sigma,\tau\}\in\mathcal{E}_{\ell}}(w_{\ell})_{\sigma\tau}.

Corollary 2 establishes the Marshall phase pattern as an exact PEC assignment for the bipartite HAF; for a given sublattice VAV_{A}, an example of this assignment is given by ϕσ=π​NA↑​(σ)\phi_{\sigma}=\pi N_{A}^{\uparrow}(\sigma) (35). The same assignment also minimizes the phase-dependent energy when the NN couplings are antiferromagnetic, and the NNN couplings are ferromagnetic, provided the NNN bonds connect sites within the same physical sublattice. An NN exchange changes the number of up spins on sublattice A by one, giving a phase difference of π\pi and satisfying PEC. An NNN exchange leaves this number unchanged, giving zero phase difference and satisfying ZEC. Both contributions therefore attain their lower bounds simultaneously for fixed amplitudes. Thus, the mixed AFM–FM model is sign-unfrustrated, even when its HG is non-bipartite. We emphasize that Marshall’s original proof [41] proceeds by contradiction and does not use the graph-theoretical viewpoint adopted here.

For the bipartite HG, PEC holds globally; hence all edges are cut, as shown in Fig. 3. An odd cycle cannot fully satisfy the PEC and therefore leads to at least one ZEC edge; the geometric frustration in the HG is thus this topological obstruction to achieving global PEC. Moreover, under frustration, the amplitudes assume a role they did not have before. The set of violated edges is no longer empty, and the best choice of which edges to leave violated depends on the weights wσ​τw_{\sigma\tau}; different amplitude profiles result in different optimal sign structures for the same HG. Consequently, when frustration is present, the solution to PRP depends on the amplitudes. For a given choice of amplitudes, minimizing EqE_{q} with respect to assignments in {0,π}\{0,\pi\} becomes a global optimization problem, equivalent to an Max-Cut problem on the weighted HG, as we shall show below.

IV.3 Binary PRP and Max-Cut

We will now restrict the optimization to real wavefunctions. This is equivalent to optimizing the phases over {0,π}\{0,\pi\}. This restriction is particularly useful for understanding the GS phase structure. The HAF Hamiltonian has real matrix elements; hence, we can choose real eigenvectors without loss of generality. Then, for GS amplitudes, PRP over binary values and PRP over continuous values yield the same answer, since the global minima of EqE_{q} lie at a discrete phase assignment for real GS, ignoring the global phase of the wavefunction. We define the signs,

sσ=ei​ϕσ∈{+1,−1},ϕσ∈{0,π}.s_{\sigma}=e^{i\phi_{\sigma}}\in\{+1,-1\},\qquad\phi_{\sigma}\in\{0,\pi\}.

Then cos⁡(ϕσ−ϕτ)\cos(\phi_{\sigma}-\phi_{\tau}) can be replaced with sσ​sτs_{\sigma}s_{\tau} and

Eℓ,q=∑{σ,τ}∈ℰℓ(wℓ)σ​τ​sσ​sτ,(wℓ)σ​τ≥0.E_{\ell,q}=\sum_{\{\sigma,\tau\}\in\mathcal{E}_{\ell}}(w_{\ell})_{\sigma\tau}\,s_{\sigma}s_{\tau},\qquad(w_{\ell})_{\sigma\tau}\geq 0.

The quantum part of the energy functional therefore defines a classical antiferromagnetic Ising model on the HG [75]. For a fixed amplitude profile, finding the signs that minimize the energy is equivalent to a QUBO instance [38]. When weights are generated from GS amplitudes, the relevant sector is ℓ=N/2\ell=N/2, or the zero-magnetization sector, since this sector is guaranteed to contain a GS for an even number of spins, as shown in Sec. II.3.

Since the amplitudes are held fixed for PRP, the edge weights are also fixed. Minimizing the Ising energy is then equivalent to maximizing the corresponding weighted cut. Similar to Sec. IV.1, any assignment {sσ}\{s_{\sigma}\} divides the vertices of Γℓ​(G)\Gamma_{\ell}(G) into two sets and thus defines a cut. An edge {σ,τ}\{\sigma,\tau\} contributes −(wℓ)σ​τ-(w_{\ell})_{\sigma\tau} to Eℓ,qE_{\ell,q}, if σ\sigma and τ\tau lie on opposite sides of the cut, i.e. sσ​sτ=−1s_{\sigma}s_{\tau}=-1, and +(wℓ)σ​τ+(w_{\ell})_{\sigma\tau} if they lie on the same side, i.e. sσ​sτ=+1s_{\sigma}s_{\tau}=+1. Similar to Eq. (42) we define the cut value in this case as,

Cutwℓ​(s)=∑{σ,τ}∈ℰℓ(wℓ)σ​τ​1−sσ​sτ2,\mathrm{Cut}_{w_{\ell}}(s)=\sum_{\{\sigma,\tau\}\in\mathcal{E}_{\ell}}(w_{\ell})_{\sigma\tau}\,\frac{1-s_{\sigma}\,s_{\tau}}{2}, (50)

and the energy can then be written as,

Eℓ,q​(s)=∑{σ,τ}∈ℰℓ(wℓ)σ​τ−2​Cutwℓ​(s).E_{\ell,q}(s)=\sum_{\{\sigma,\tau\}\in\mathcal{E}_{\ell}}(w_{\ell})_{\sigma\tau}-2\,\mathrm{Cut}_{w_{\ell}}(s). (51)

Since the first term in Eq. (51) is constant, minimizing Eℓ,qE_{\ell,q} is equivalent to maximizing the cut value Cutwℓ​(s)\mathrm{Cut}_{w_{\ell}}(s). Binary PRP is therefore an instance of weighted Max-Cut on the HG, leading to the following theorem.

Theorem 5 (Heisenberg-Ising Correspondence).

Binary or {0,π}\{0,\pi\} PRP of HAF defined on a physical graph G in sector ℓ\ell, is equivalent to determining the GS of a classical antiferromagnetic Ising model on Γℓ​(G)\Gamma_{\ell}(G), which in turn is equivalent to a weighted Max-Cut problem on Γℓ​(G)\Gamma_{\ell}(G).

In this correspondence, the Ising interaction on the HG arises from the interference between two basis configurations connected by the off-diagonal Heisenberg exchange: in the binary sector, the relative phase of this interfering pair is encoded by the product of two sign variables attached to the corresponding HG vertices. Consequently, finding the optimal binary sign structure is the GS problem of this weighted antiferromagnetic Ising model, or equivalently, the weighted Max-Cut problem on the amplitude-weighted HG, illustrated in Fig. 1.

Each binary PRP of HAF maps, in polynomial time, to a Max-Cut instance on Γℓ​(G)\Gamma_{\ell}(G) carrying the weights induced by the amplitudes through Eq. (45). This polynomial-time reduction can be written as

Binary PRP≤pMax-Cut,\textsf{Binary~}\textsf{PRP}\leq_{\mathrm{p}}\textsf{Max-Cut}, (52)

meaning that any polynomial-time algorithm for weighted Max-Cut would immediately yield one for binary PRP. The relation (52) bounds the difficulty of PRP only from above: it shows that PRP is at most as hard as weighted Max-Cut, but does not, by itself, establish NP-hardness.

A true hardness statement would require the reverse reduction, Max-Cut≤pBinary PRP\textsf{Max-Cut}\leq_{\mathrm{p}}\textsf{Binary }\textsf{PRP}, namely a polynomial-time encoding of an arbitrary Max-Cut instance into a PRP instance. The HG of a HAF is a token graph; hence, it has a very specific structure. So it is not obvious that for Max-Cut defined any graph we can find an isomorphic HG. Moreover, the weights come from the amplitudes and thus have a specific structure.

Nevertheless, we can map Max-Cut on arbitrary graph to binary PRP on an HG by using the one-magnon sector, or ℓ=1\ell=1. This happens because in the one-magnon sector, the HG is isomorphic to its parent graph (Fig. 4). If we use the Heisenberg model of Eq. 33 then for an NN-spin system, fixing ψσ=1​∀σ∈𝒱1\psi_{\sigma}=1\,\forall\sigma\in\mathcal{V}_{1}, it follows directly from Eq. (45) that

(w1)σ​τ=Ji​j/N∀σ​⇌i​j​τ.(w_{1})_{\sigma\tau}=J_{ij}/N\quad\forall\sigma\overset{ij}{\rightleftharpoons}\tau. (53)

Thus, the parent graph weights get inherited by its HG. This implies that, by setting the right coupling values, we can map any Max-Cut in GG to an equal-amplitude binary PRP in Γ1​(G)\Gamma_{1}(G). By the duality (12) the same argument also covers ℓ=N−1\ell=N-1. Ref. [65] we classifies the complexity of unweighted Max-Cut on HG as a function of ℓ\ell. Notable results are: for a fixed constant value of ℓ\ell, unweighted Max-Cut on HG is NP-hard in the size of the physical graph, and for ℓ≥Nδ,δ>0\ell\geq N^{\delta},\delta>0, unweighted Max-Cut on HG is not NP-hard in the size of the HG if a quasipolynomial counterpart of the hypothesis NP⊆P/poly\textsf{NP}\subseteq\mathrm{P}/\mathrm{poly} holds true.

V Optimization Methods

Many algorithms have been developed for solving Max-Cut. Here we focus on two that are intricately tied to studying Max-Cut on HG: the Rank-2 relaxation and the GW algorithm. The Rank-2 relaxation is already present in the quantum mechanical expectation value of the energy and the GW algorithm is capable of producing exact GS sign structure in time polynomial in the size of the HG, as we will discuss in the following sections.

V.1 Rank-2 Relaxation

In this section we study PRP without restricting the phases. Here, we minimize the weighted XY energy Eq​(ϕ)E_{q}(\phi) of Eq. (44) on the HG with fixed weights by continuously optimizing the phases. The phases form points on a circle, as shown in Fig. 5. This optimization is similar to the Rank-2 relaxation method of Burer et al. [11] for solving Max-Cut. Rank-2 relaxation was introduced as a cheap method for approximating Max-Cut of weighted graphs. We, however, arrived at this method from a purely quantum-mechanical perspective; the complex wavefunction and the Hamiltonian’s Hermiticity force the Rank-2 form of Eq. (44). But Rank-2 relaxation is defined for any weighted graph, whereas PRP is defined on weighted HG. In the one-magnon sector, however, PRP and Rank-2 relaxation are equivalent. This is because Γ1​(G)≅G\Gamma_{1}(G)\cong G and Eq. (53) implies that for equal amplitude PRP in one magnon sector one can always choose couplings of the Hamiltonian (33) such that arbitrary weighted Max-Cut on GG can also be realized on Γ1​(G)\Gamma_{1}(G).

The phase-dependent part of any variational ansatz in sector ℓ\ell with continuously parameterized phases is Eℓ,qE_{\ell,q}. However, not all variational ansätze allow independent changes to amplitudes (hence weights) and phases. Only mod-phase networks allow that [66]. Then, for these networks, using the Rank-2 relaxation formulation, we can extract information about the energy landscape in the phase sector, treating phase and amplitude as independent parameters. We discuss this in detail later; for now, we introduce basic properties of Rank-2 relaxation. We ask what the landscape of Eq​(ϕ)E_{q}(\phi) looks like, namely its stationary points, their character, and how the discrete {0,π}\{0,\pi\} assignments sit inside the continuum. The objective of Rank-2 relaxation is minimization of

minϕσ∈ℝ⁡Eℓ,q​(ϕ)=min⁡∑{σ,τ}∈ℰℓϕσ∈ℝ⁡(wℓ)σ​τ​cos⁡(ϕσ−ϕτ),\min_{\phi_{\sigma}\in\mathbb{R}}E_{\ell,q}(\phi)=\min_{\phi_{\sigma}\in\mathbb{R}}\sum_{\{\sigma,\tau\}\in\mathcal{E}_{\ell}}(w_{\ell})_{\sigma\tau}\cos(\phi_{\sigma}-\phi_{\tau}), (54)

where the weights are fixed. The problem has a U⁡(1)U(1) symmetry; shifting all ϕσ\phi_{\sigma} by a global phase does not change the energy. Rank-2 relaxation first finds minima of Eℓ,qE_{\ell,q} using gradient descent methods, then applies a rounding method to convert phases to binary values, ±1\pm 1. The minimization part is PRP and the rounding part is binary PRP. The details of the algorithm are given in Algorithm V.1. The gradient of Eℓ,qE_{\ell,q} with respect to the phase is given by,

∂Eℓ,q∂ϕσ=−∑τ∈𝒩⁡(σ)(wℓ)σ​τsin(ϕσ−ϕτ),\frac{\partial E_{\ell,q}}{\partial\phi_{\sigma}}=-\sum_{\tau\in\mathcal{N}(\sigma)}(w_{\ell})_{\sigma\tau}\,\sin(\phi_{\sigma}-\phi_{\tau}), (55)

Minimizing Eℓ,qE_{\ell,q} with respect to the phases {ϕσ}\{\phi_{\sigma}\} yields the Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT) [28, 32] stationary conditions

∑τ∈𝒩⁡(σ)(wℓ)σ​τ​sin⁡(ϕσ−ϕτ)=0,∀σ∈𝒱ℓ.\sum_{\tau\in\mathcal{N}(\sigma)}(w_{\ell})_{\sigma\tau}\,\sin(\phi_{\sigma}-\phi_{\tau})=0,\qquad\forall\,\sigma\in\mathcal{V}_{\ell}. (56)

The solutions of these equations correspond to zero gradients of Eℓ,qE_{\ell,q} with respect to ϕσ\phi_{\sigma}. The discrete phase assignment ϕσ∈{0,π}\phi_{\sigma}\in\{0,\pi\} (modulo 2​π2\pi) is an obvious solution of the stationarity equations. For nn states, there are 2n2^{n} such discrete phase assignments. Whenever a variational ansatz can realize such an assignment, these solutions also correspond to zero gradients of Eℓ,qE_{\ell,q} with respect to the ansatz’s variational parameters, provided the amplitudes are held fixed, by the chain rule. Moreover, if {ϕσ}\{\phi_{\sigma}\} is a solution, then {ϕσ+δ}\{\phi_{\sigma}+\delta\} is also a solution for any constant δ\delta. As a result, these {0,π}\{0,\pi\} assignments organize into 2n−12^{n-1} distinct one-parameter families (“lines”) in the phase space (modulo 2​π2\pi) that correspond to stationary points of Eℓ,qE_{\ell,q}. In general, there can be stationary points that do not correspond to a {0,π}\{0,\pi\} assignment.

The local character of the stationary points is determined by the Hessian

∂2Eℓ,q∂ϕσ​∂ϕτ={−∑μ∈𝒩⁡(σ)(wℓ)σ​μcos(ϕσ−ϕμ),σ=τ,(wℓ)σ​τ​cos⁡(ϕσ−ϕτ),{σ,τ}∈ℰℓ,0,otherwise.\frac{\partial^{2}E_{\ell,q}}{\partial\phi_{\sigma}\partial\phi_{\tau}}=\begin{cases}-\sum_{\mu\in\mathcal{N}(\sigma)}(w_{\ell})_{\sigma\mu}\cos(\phi_{\sigma}-\phi_{\mu}),&\sigma=\tau,\\ \displaystyle(w_{\ell})_{\sigma\tau}\cos(\phi_{\sigma}-\phi_{\tau}),&\{\sigma,\tau\}\in\mathcal{E}_{\ell},\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}

If (wℓ)σ​τ​cos⁡(ϕσ−ϕτ)≥0(w_{\ell})_{\sigma\tau}\cos(\phi_{\sigma}-\phi_{\tau})\geq 0 on every edge, then the Hessian is negative semidefinite due to diagonal dominance and the Gershgorin disk theorem; accordingly, if (wℓ)σ​τ​cos⁡(ϕσ−ϕτ)≤0(w_{\ell})_{\sigma\tau}\cos(\phi_{\sigma}-\phi_{\tau})\leq 0 on every edge, then it is positive semidefinite. In general, however, these effective couplings have mixed signs, so the Hessian need not be semidefinite and is generically indefinite. In fact, if a {0,π}\{0,\pi\} assignment does not correspond to a global minimum or maximum, then it is a saddle point (see Theorem 3.4 of Ref. [11]).

{algorithm}

[h] Rank-2 Max-Cut

1: weight matrix wi​jw_{ij} and indices i,ji,j; number of vertices nn; steps TT; Adam [29] optimizer.
2: Normalize the weights, wi​j←wi​j/max⁡(|wi​j|)w_{ij}\leftarrow w_{ij}/\mathrm{max}(|w_{ij}|).
3: Draw angles θi∈ℝ\theta_{i}\in\mathbb{R} uniformly from [0,π)[0,\pi), so that 𝐯i=(cos⁡θi,sin⁡θi)\mathbf{v}_{i}=(\cos\theta_{i},\sin\theta_{i}).
4: for t=1,…,Tt=1,\dots,T do
5:   Calculate gradient, Gi←∑j(wi​j+wj​i)​sin⁡(θj−θi)G_{i}\leftarrow\sum_{j}(w_{ij}+w_{ji})\,\sin(\theta_{j}-\theta_{i}).
6:   Update angles using optimizer, θi←θi+Adam⁡(Gi)\theta_{i}\leftarrow\theta_{i}+\mathrm{Adam}(G_{i}).
7: end for
8: Map the angles to the circle, θi←θimod2​π\theta_{i}\leftarrow\theta_{i}\bmod 2\pi.
9: Sort {βi=θimodπ}\{\beta_{i}=\theta_{i}\bmod\pi\} in ascending order as β1≤⋯≤βn\beta_{1}\leq\dots\leq\beta_{n}, and set βn+1=π\beta_{n+1}=\pi.
10: Construct the candidate cut angles, αm←(βm+βm+1)/2\alpha_{m}\leftarrow(\beta_{m}+\beta_{m+1})/2 for m=1,…,nm=1,\dots,n.
11: Construct the sign matrix, Sm​i=+1S_{mi}=+1 if θi≤αm\theta_{i}\leq\alpha_{m} or θi>αm+π\theta_{i}>\alpha_{m}+\pi, and Sm​i=−1S_{mi}=-1 otherwise.
12: Choose m=m⋆m=m^{\star} such that ∑i​jwi​j​Sm​i​Sm​j\sum_{ij}w_{ij}\,S_{mi}S_{mj} is minimum.
13: Return the sign structure, {si}\{s_{i}\} for si=Sm⋆​is_{i}=S_{m^{\star}i}.

The Rank-2 objective is non-convex, and spurious minima can trap the optimization at higher energies. Burer et al. [11] mitigate this by random restarts where after reaching a local minimum the phases are moved to the lowest energy {0,π}\{0,\pi\} assignment in its neighborhood, which is a saddle point, and the minimization is restarted from there in hope of reaching a lower minimum. But even if the global minimum is reached this way, it may not correspond to a cut, i.e., {0,π}\{0,\pi\} phase values. However, since the eigenvectors of HAF can be chosen real, when the weights are generated from GS amplitudes, the global minima are situated at a {0,π}\{0,\pi\} assignment (modulo 2​π2\pi). Therefore, the accuracy of GS PRP using Rank-2 relaxation is only limited by the quality of the gradient descent. Table 2 shows the accuracy of Rank-2 relaxation for GS weights. Here, the Adam [29] optimizer was used for gradient descent without random restarts, and the results in Table 2 imply that the optimizer was able to reach very close to the global minima.

The Rank-2 relaxation maps discrete binary-valued signs to points on a unit circle. One can also map the signs to a higher-dimensional sphere, which leads to the next section.

V.2 Goemans–Williamson Relaxation

The Goemans–Williamson (GW) algorithm [22] replaces the Ising spins sσ∈{±1}s_{\sigma}\in\{\pm 1\} of Eq. (50) with unit vectors 𝐯σ∈ℝ|𝒱ℓ|\mathbf{v}_{\sigma}\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{V}_{\ell}|}. Using 𝐯σ⋅𝐯τ\mathbf{v}_{\sigma}\cdot\mathbf{v}_{\tau} as a continuous proxy for sσ​sτs_{\sigma}s_{\tau}, it relaxes Max-Cut to

max⁡∑{σ,τ}∈ℰℓ‖𝐯σ‖=1⁡(wℓ)σ​τ​(1−𝐯σ⋅𝐯τ2)\max_{\|\mathbf{v}_{\sigma}\|=1}\sum_{\{\sigma,\tau\}\in\mathcal{E}_{\ell}}(w_{\ell})_{\sigma\tau}\left(\frac{1-\mathbf{v}_{\sigma}\cdot\mathbf{v}_{\tau}}{2}\right) (57)

Equivalently, define the Gram matrix X∈ℝ|𝒱ℓ|×|𝒱ℓ|X\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{V}_{\ell}|\times|\mathcal{V}_{\ell}|} by

Xσ​τ=𝐯σ⋅𝐯τ,∀σ,τ∈𝒱ℓX_{\sigma\tau}=\mathbf{v}_{\sigma}\cdot\mathbf{v}_{\tau},\qquad\forall\sigma,\tau\in\mathcal{V}_{\ell} (58)

so that X=Y⊤​YX=Y^{\top}Y, where Y∈ℝ|𝒱ℓ|×|𝒱ℓ|Y\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{V}_{\ell}|\times|\mathcal{V}_{\ell}|} is the matrix whose σ\sigma-th column is 𝐯σ\mathbf{v}_{\sigma}. By construction, X⪰0X\succeq 0 and diag⁡(X)=I\mathrm{diag}(X)=I. The relaxed Max-Cut then becomes the following SDP.

max⁡∑{σ,τ}∈ℰℓX⪰0,Xσ​σ=1⁡(wℓ)σ​τ​(1−Xσ​τ2)\max_{X\succeq 0,\,X_{\sigma\sigma}=1}\sum_{\{\sigma,\tau\}\in\mathcal{E}_{\ell}}(w_{\ell})_{\sigma\tau}\left(\frac{1-X_{\sigma\tau}}{2}\right) (59)

Any sign assignment {sσ}\{s_{\sigma}\} can be realized by this relaxation using 𝐯σ=sσ​𝐮\mathbf{v}_{\sigma}=s_{\sigma}\mathbf{u}, where u^\hat{u} is a fixed unit vector. Thus, the maximum of the relaxed problem is at-least as large as the Max-Cut. This convex program can be solved in polynomial time to obtain an optimal solution X⋆X^{\star}, which can be factorized, for example via Cholesky or eigen decomposition, as X⋆=(Y⋆)⊤​Y⋆X^{\star}=(Y^{\star})^{\top}Y^{\star}, yielding a set of unit vectors {𝐯σ⋆}\{\mathbf{v}^{\star}_{\sigma}\}.

The SDP solution thus gives a set of unit vectors {𝐯σ⋆}\{\mathbf{v}^{\star}_{\sigma}\} instead of the Ising spins ±1\pm 1. GW converts the vectors into Ising spins using a random hyperplane through the origin: (i) Sample a random direction 𝐫\mathbf{r} uniformly from the unit sphere. (ii) Assign a spin by the sign of the projection:

sσ=sign⁡(𝐫⋅𝐯σ⋆)s_{\sigma}=\mathrm{sign}(\mathbf{r}\cdot\mathbf{v}^{\star}_{\sigma})

Geometrically, the hyperplane perpendicular to 𝐫\mathbf{r} separates the hypersphere into two hemispheres; vertices of an edge landing on opposite hemispheres form a cut. For an edge {σ,τ}\{\sigma,\tau\}, if the angle between vσv_{\sigma} and vτv_{\tau} is θσ​τ∈[0,π]\theta_{\sigma\tau}\in[0,\pi], then the probability that the hyperplane separates them is Pr[sσ≠sτ]=θσ​τπ\mathrm{Pr}[s_{\sigma}\neq s_{\tau}]=\tfrac{\theta_{\sigma\tau}}{\pi}. Hence, the expected rounded cut value is

𝔼⁡[Cut​(s)]=∑(σ,τ)∈ℰℓ(wℓ)σ​τ​θσ​τπ\mathbb{E}[\textsf{Cut}(s)]=\sum_{(\sigma,\tau)\in\mathcal{E}_{\ell}}(w_{\ell})_{\sigma\tau}\frac{\theta_{\sigma\tau}}{\pi} (60)

Goemans and Williamson showed that for all θσ​τ\theta_{\sigma\tau},

θσ​τ/π(1−cos⁡θσ​τ)/2≥αGW,\frac{\theta_{\sigma\tau}/\pi}{(1-\cos\theta_{\sigma\tau})/2}\geq\alpha_{\textsf{GW}}, (61)

where αGW≈0.87856\alpha_{\textsf{GW}}\approx 0.87856. This bound leads to the following relation for non-negative edge weights, i.e., (wℓ)σ​τ≥0(w_{\ell})_{\sigma\tau}\geq 0.
