𝔼⁡[Cut​(s)]≥αGW​∑{σ,τ}∈ℰℓ(wℓ)σ​τ​(1−Xσ​τ⋆2)\mathbb{E}[\textsf{Cut}(s)]\geq\alpha_{\textsf{GW}}\sum_{\{\sigma,\tau\}\in\mathcal{E}_{\ell}}(w_{\ell})_{\sigma\tau}\left(\frac{1-X^{\star}_{\sigma\tau}}{2}\right)

Thus, the random-hyperplane rounding produces a cut whose expected value is at least 87.8%87.8\% of Max-Cut. The GW algorithm solves an SDP with a symmetric |𝒱ℓ|×|𝒱ℓ||\mathcal{V}_{\ell}|\times|\mathcal{V}_{\ell}| positive-semidefinite matrix. This means the algorithm deals with 𝒪⁡(|𝒱ℓ|2)\mathcal{O}(|\mathcal{V}_{\ell}|^{2}) variational parameters. In contrast, Rank-2 relaxation uses 𝒪⁡(|𝒱ℓ|)\mathcal{O}(|\mathcal{V}_{\ell}|) parameters but has a non-convex optimization landscape. Therefore, we must choose between computational efficiency and theoretical performance guarantees. However, Table 2 shows that for GS PRP, the Rank-2 relaxation can produce high-quality solutions despite being non-convex. Ref. [11] has also found that Rank-2 can produce high-quality approximate solutions while being significantly faster than the native GW implementation. Moreover, the size of HG grows exponentially when ℓ\ell is linear in the number of spins, which means the native GW implementation becomes memory-constrained for large system sizes much faster than Rank-2.

For these reasons, we have chosen the Burer-Monteiro (BM) factorization [9, 10] as a cheap method to implement the GW algorithm. The BM factorization involves optimization over a k×|𝒱ℓ|k\times|\mathcal{V}_{\ell}| matrix, YY, for X=YT​YX=Y^{T}Y. In other words, the BM factorization assumes that it is optimal for the vectors 𝐯σ⋆\mathbf{v}^{\star}_{\sigma} to be kk-dimensional. XX is positive semidefinite by construction in this case, and Xσ​σ=1X_{\sigma\sigma}=1 is achieved by forcing the vectors to be of unit length. However, when optimizing over YY instead of XX, we lose convexity, and second-order critical points appear. Boumal et al. [6] have shown that as long as k≥⌈2​|𝒱ℓ|⌉k\geq\lceil\sqrt{2|\mathcal{V}_{\ell}|}\,\rceil, the second order critical points are also global minima and Waldspurger and Waters [72] have shown that this bound is tight. Thus we can effectively reduce the number of variables to 𝒪⁡(|𝒱ℓ|1.5)\mathcal{O}(|\mathcal{V}_{\ell}|^{1.5}) while retaining the performance guarantee of the GW algorithm. The implementation details for BM factorization are given in Algorithm V.2. The results in Table 2 imply that the optimizer was able to reproduce GS signs faithfully.

{algorithm}

[h] GW algorithm via BM factorization

1: weight matrix wi​jw_{ij} and indices i,ji,j; number of vertices nn, rank kk; hyperplanes nhn_{h}; steps TT; Adam [29] optimizer.
2: Normalize the weights, wi​j←wi​j/max⁡(|wi​j|)w_{ij}\leftarrow w_{ij}/\mathrm{max}(|w_{ij}|).
3: Draw V∈ℝk×nV\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times n} from a random distribution.
4: Normalize the column vectors of VV, 𝐯i←𝐯i/|𝐯i|\mathbf{v}_{i}\leftarrow\mathbf{v}_{i}/|\mathbf{v}_{i}|.
5: for t=1,…,Tt=1,\dots,T do
6:   Calculate gradient, 𝐆i←∑j(wi​j+wj​i)​𝐯j\mathbf{G}_{i}\leftarrow\sum_{j}(w_{ij}+w_{ji})\,\mathbf{v}_{j}.
7:   Discard the radial part, 𝐆i←𝐆i−(𝐆i⋅𝐯i)​𝐯i\mathbf{G}_{i}\leftarrow\mathbf{G}_{i}-(\mathbf{G}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{v}_{i})\,\mathbf{v}_{i}.
8:   Update vectors, 𝐯i←𝐯i+Adam⁡(𝐆i)\mathbf{v}_{i}\leftarrow\mathbf{v}_{i}+\mathrm{Adam}(\mathbf{G}_{i}).
9:   Normalize the vectors after update, 𝐯i←𝐯i/|𝐯i|\mathbf{v}_{i}\leftarrow\mathbf{v}_{i}/|\mathbf{v}_{i}|.
10: end for
11: Draw nhn_{h}, kk-dimensional random vectors, {𝐫m}\{\mathbf{r}_{m}\}.
12: Construct the sign matrix Sm​i=sign⁡(𝐫m⋅𝐯i)S_{mi}=\mathrm{sign}(\mathbf{r}_{m}\cdot\mathbf{v}_{i}).
13: Choose m=m⋆m=m^{\star} such that ∑i​jwi​j​Sm​i​Sm​j\sum_{ij}w_{ij}\,S_{mi}S_{mj} is minimum.
14: Return the sign structure, {si}\{s_{i}\} for si=Sm⋆​is_{i}=S_{m^{\star}i}.

For GS PRP where the weights are generated from GS amplitudes, the GW algorithm can recover the GS signs exactly. This is because for GS weights all the optimal vectors, 𝐯σ⋆\mathbf{v}^{\star}_{\sigma}, are collinear and their directions correspond to the GS sign structure. Hence the GW algorithm can realize the Max-Cut exactly, i.e., just like the Rank-2 case the integrality gap is zero, and a hyperplane that does not contain the rank-11 solutions can reproduce the GS signs exactly. We prove this fact in the following section.

V.3 Time Complexity of Max-Cut for Non-Degenerate GS

The GW relaxation offers a straightforward way to determine how difficult it is to reconstruct the sign structure using Max-Cut when the weights come from GS amplitudes. The approach in this section does not rely on the specific form of the Hamiltonian. As long as we are working in a finite-dimensional vector space with a real Hamiltonian, the proof applies.

In this proof we use the matrix representation of the HAF in sector ℓ\ell, HℓH_{\ell}, with orthonormal basis 𝒱ℓ\mathcal{V}_{\ell}. However, they can be replaced with any real Hamiltonian matrix represented in an orthonormal basis. For the rest of this section, we will also assume the wavefunction is normalized for simplicity. Since HℓH_{\ell} is real, its eigenvectors can also be taken as real. Let

|ΨGS⟩=∑σ∈𝒱ℓsσ​ψσ​|σ⟩,sσ=±1,ψσ≥0,\ket{\Psi_{\mathrm{GS}}}=\sum_{\sigma\in\mathcal{V}_{\ell}}s_{\sigma}\psi_{\sigma}\ket{\sigma},\qquad s_{\sigma}=\pm 1,\psi_{\sigma}\geq 0,

be the non-degenerate GS of HℓH_{\ell} with energy E0E_{0}. When doing GS PRP using GW algorithm, without any loss of generality we can say that the algorithm minimizes the following function with respect to XX in Eq. (58)

EGW=∑σ,τ∈𝒱ℓψσ​ψτ​(Hℓ)σ​τ​Xσ​τs.t.Xσ​σ=1,X⪰0.E_{\textsf{GW}}=\sum_{\sigma,\tau\in\mathcal{V}_{\ell}}\psi_{\sigma}\psi_{\tau}(H_{\ell})_{\sigma\tau}X_{\sigma\tau}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad X_{\sigma\sigma}=1,\,X\succeq 0.

The proof proceeds as follows. First, we show that the minima of EGWE_{\mathrm{GW}} equal the GS energy, E0E_{0}. At the minima, the vectors vσv_{\sigma} are collinear; thus, choosing a hyperplane that does not contain this line will reproduce the GS signs exactly. We then show that it is sufficient to reach within a small region of the minima to reproduce the GS signs. Minimizing GW with respect to XX is convex, so we can always get arbitrarily close to the minima [2]. Thus, the time complexity depends on the number of steps required to reach such a region.

We start by determining a lower bound on EGWE_{\textsf{GW}}. Define a symmetric matrix,

ρσ​τ=ψσ​ψτ​Xσ​τ.\rho_{\sigma\tau}=\psi_{\sigma}\psi_{\tau}X_{\sigma\tau}.

For Dψ=diag⁡(ψσ0,ψσ1,…,ψσ|𝒱ℓ|−1)D_{\psi}=\mathrm{diag}(\psi_{\sigma_{0}},\psi_{\sigma_{1}},\ldots,\psi_{\sigma_{|\mathcal{V}_{\ell}|-1}}), ρ=Dψ​X​Dψ\rho=D_{\psi}\,X\,D_{\psi}. Since X⪰0X\succeq 0 it implies ρ⪰0\rho\succeq 0, as for any vector μ\mu, μT​ρ​μ=(Dψ​μ)T​X​(Dψ​μ)≥0\mu^{T}\rho\mu=(D_{\psi}\mu)^{T}X(D_{\psi}\mu)\geq 0. Also, Tr⁡(ρ)=1\operatorname{Tr}(\rho)=1 as ρσ​σ=ψσ2\rho_{\sigma\sigma}=\psi_{\sigma}^{2}. Thus, ρ\rho is a valid density matrix. Consider the orthonormal eigendecomposition of ρ\rho, guaranteed by the spectral theorem.

ρ=∑α=0|𝒱ℓ|−1pα​|pα⟩​⟨pα|,\rho=\sum_{\alpha=0}^{|\mathcal{V}_{\ell}|-1}p_{\alpha}\ket{p_{\alpha}}\bra{p_{\alpha}}, (62)

where |pα⟩\ket{p_{\alpha}} are the eigenfunctions of ρ\rho with eigenvalues pα≥0p_{\alpha}\geq 0 as ρ⪰0\rho\succeq 0 and ∑αpα=Tr⁡(ρ)=1\sum_{\alpha}p_{\alpha}=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho)=1. Then,

EGW=Tr⁡(Hℓ​ρ)=∑αpα​⟨pα|Hℓ|pα⟩E_{\textsf{GW}}=\operatorname{Tr}(H_{\ell}\,\rho)=\sum_{\alpha}p_{\alpha}\braket{p_{\alpha}|H_{\ell}|p_{\alpha}} (63)

But the energy of any state in the vector space spanned by 𝒱ℓ\mathcal{V}_{\ell} is bounded below by the GS energy of HℓH_{\ell}. Thus,

EGW≥E0,E_{\textsf{GW}}\geq E_{0},

with equality achieved only when |pα⟩\ket{p_{\alpha}} are GS for all pα≠0p_{\alpha}\neq 0. When the GS is non-degenerate, there is only one choice of the density matrix for the equality, and that is a pure state constructed from the GS,

ρ=|ΨGS⟩​⟨ΨGS|.\rho=\ket{\Psi_{\mathrm{GS}}}\bra{\Psi_{\mathrm{GS}}}.

Comparing the non-zero matrix elements, we get,

Xσ​τ=𝐯σ⋅𝐯τ=sσ​sτ=±1,∀ψσ​ψτ≠0X_{\sigma\tau}=\mathbf{v}_{\sigma}\cdot\mathbf{v}_{\tau}=s_{\sigma}s_{\tau}=\pm 1,\quad\forall\,\psi_{\sigma}\psi_{\tau}\neq 0

If any ψσ=0\psi_{\sigma}=0 then it will lead to a corresponding column and row of ρ\rho being zero. The signs for these zero amplitudes can be chosen arbitrarily without affecting the energy, hence their values do not matter. The form of XX above is a valid solution as it satisfies Xσ​σ=1X_{\sigma\sigma}=1 and X⪰0X\succeq 0. The latter follows from X=𝐬​𝐬TX=\mathbf{s}\,\mathbf{s}^{T}, where 𝐬\mathbf{s} is the column vector of GS signs. The equation above also implies that the optimal values of 𝐯σ\mathbf{v}_{\sigma} for vertices with non-zero amplitudes are collinear. In other words, sσ​𝐯σs_{\sigma}\mathbf{v}_{\sigma} points in the same direction for all ψσ≠0\psi_{\sigma}\neq 0. Then choosing a hyperplane perpendicular to this line will reproduce the exact GS sign structure.

In reality, SDP solvers are not guaranteed to reach the minima exactly, but they are guaranteed to reach within a certain bound in finite steps. Let us assume that we are within a certain distance of the ground state energy, quantified in the error measure

ϵ=EGW−E0≥0.\epsilon=E_{\textsf{GW}}-E_{0}\geq 0.

In this case, 𝐯σ\mathbf{v}_{\sigma} are not guaranteed to be collinear, and neither is ρ\rho guaranteed to be a pure state. We want ϵ\epsilon small enough to still recover the GS signs. Since the hyperplane is no longer unique, we choose it to be perpendicular to a vector with nonzero amplitude, say 𝐯σr\mathbf{v}_{\sigma_{r}}. Then, the condition for reproducing the GS signs is

sσ​𝐯σ⋅sσr​𝐯σr>0,∀ψσ≠0.s_{\sigma}\mathbf{v}_{\sigma}\cdot s_{\sigma_{r}}\mathbf{v}_{\sigma_{r}}>0,\quad\forall\psi_{\sigma}\neq 0. (64)

Consider the probability-averaged direction defined as

𝐮=∑σ∈𝒱ℓψσ2​sσ​𝐯σ.\mathbf{u}=\sum_{\sigma\in\mathcal{V}_{\ell}}\psi_{\sigma}^{2}s_{\sigma}\mathbf{v}_{\sigma}.

We will use this direction as a reference. The GS signs sσs_{\sigma} are required to construct this vector, which we do not know yet. However, we do not need to calculate the signs as the upper bound on ϵ\epsilon will not depend on them, we only require the existence of the GS signs. The magnitude of 𝐮\mathbf{u} is connected with the energy, as we will show now. By the spectral theorem, let |Ei⟩\ket{E_{i}} be the orthonormal eigenvectors of HH with eigenvalues EiE_{i} such that Ei+1≥EiE_{i+1}\geq E_{i}. Then, using |pα⟩=∑i⟨Ei|pα⟩​|Ei⟩\ket{p_{\alpha}}=\sum_{i}\braket{E_{i}|p_{\alpha}}\ket{E_{i}} in (63),

EGW=∑i,αpα​|⟨Ei|pα⟩|2​Ei.E_{\textsf{GW}}=\sum_{i,\alpha}p_{\alpha}\left\lvert\braket{E_{i}|p_{\alpha}}\right\rvert^{2}E_{i}. (65)

Since E0<E1≤…≤E|𝒱ℓ|−1E_{0}<E_{1}\leq\ldots\leq E_{|\mathcal{V}_{\ell}|-1} and ∑i≥1|⟨Ei|pα⟩|2=1−|⟨E0|pα⟩|2\sum_{i\geq 1}\left\lvert\braket{E_{i}|p_{\alpha}}\right\rvert^{2}=1-\left\lvert\braket{E_{0}|p_{\alpha}}\right\rvert^{2}, we get the following inequality from Eq. (65) by replacing Ei>1E_{i>1} with E1E_{1}, as follows:

ϵ≥(1−∑αpα​|⟨E0|pα⟩|2)​(E1−E0),\epsilon\geq\left(1-\sum_{\alpha}p_{\alpha}\left\lvert\braket{E_{0}|p_{\alpha}}\right\rvert^{2}\right)(E_{1}-E_{0}), (66)

and the square of the magnitude of 𝐮\mathbf{u} is given by,

|𝐮|2\displaystyle|\mathbf{u}|^{2} =∑σ,τ∈𝒱ℓψσ2​ψτ2​sσ​sτ​𝐯σ⋅𝐯τ,\displaystyle=\sum_{\sigma,\tau\in\mathcal{V}_{\ell}}\psi_{\sigma}^{2}\psi_{\tau}^{2}s_{\sigma}s_{\tau}\mathbf{v}_{\sigma}\cdot\mathbf{v}_{\tau},
=⟨E0|ρ|E0⟩=∑αpα​|⟨E0|pα⟩|2.\displaystyle=\braket{E_{0}|\rho|E_{0}}=\sum_{\alpha}p_{\alpha}\left\lvert\braket{E_{0}|p_{\alpha}}\right\rvert^{2}.

Putting this value in (66) we get,

|𝐮|≥1−ϵE1−E0≥1−ϵE1−E0.|\mathbf{u}|\geq\sqrt{1-\frac{\epsilon}{E_{1}-E_{0}}}\geq 1-\frac{\epsilon}{E_{1}-E_{0}}. (67)

Here we assume ϵ<E1−E0\epsilon<E_{1}-E_{0} which also implies that 𝐮≠0\mathbf{u}\neq 0. Now, let us decompose sσ​𝐯σs_{\sigma}\mathbf{v}_{\sigma} into parallel and perpendicular parts:

sσ𝐯σ=cosθσ𝐮^+sinθσ𝐧^σ,s_{\sigma}\mathbf{v}_{\sigma}=\cos\theta_{\sigma}\,\hat{\mathbf{u}}+\sin\theta_{\sigma}\,\hat{\mathbf{n}}_{\sigma}, (68)

where 𝐮^=𝐮/|𝐮|\hat{\mathbf{u}}={\mathbf{u}}/{|\mathbf{u}|} and 𝐧^σ\hat{\mathbf{n}}_{\sigma} is a unit vector perpendicular to 𝐮^\hat{\mathbf{u}}. The angle sσ​𝐯σs_{\sigma}\mathbf{v}_{\sigma} makes with 𝐮\mathbf{u} is θσ\theta_{\sigma}. From the inequality 𝐧^σ⋅𝐧^σr≥−1\hat{\mathbf{n}}_{\sigma}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}}_{\sigma_{r}}\geq-1 and Eq. (68) it follows that,

sσ​𝐯σ⋅sσr​𝐯σr≥cos⁡(θσ+θσr).s_{\sigma}\mathbf{v}_{\sigma}\cdot s_{\sigma_{r}}\mathbf{v}_{\sigma_{r}}\geq\cos(\theta_{\sigma}+\theta_{\sigma_{r}}).

Comparing this with (64) we conclude that for reconstructing the GS signs exactly, it is sufficient to satisfy

0≤θσ<π/4∀ψσ≠0.0\leq\theta_{\sigma}<\pi/4\quad\forall\psi_{\sigma}\neq 0. (69)

The spread in the angles θσ\theta_{\sigma} is directly determined by ϵ\epsilon, the smaller the ϵ\epsilon the smaller the spread. Our task now is to determine the upper bound on ϵ\epsilon such that (69) is maintained. Determining |𝐮||\mathbf{u}| in terms of the angles, we get the following relation

|𝐮|=𝐮^⋅𝐮=∑σ∈𝒱ℓψσ2cosθσ.|\mathbf{u}|=\hat{\mathbf{u}}\cdot\mathbf{u}=\sum_{\sigma\in\mathcal{V}_{\ell}}\psi_{\sigma}^{2}\cos\theta_{\sigma}.

Using this in Eq. (67)

1−|𝐮|=∑σ∈𝒱ℓψσ2​(1−cos⁡θσ)≤ϵE1−E0.1-|\mathbf{u}|=\sum_{\sigma\in\mathcal{V}_{\ell}}\psi_{\sigma}^{2}(1-\cos\theta_{\sigma})\leq\frac{\epsilon}{E_{1}-E_{0}}.

Since ψσ2​(1−cos⁡θσ)\psi_{\sigma}^{2}(1-\cos\theta_{\sigma}) is always non-negative, the inequality implies that each term inside the sum cannot exceed the upper bound.

ψσ2​(1−cos⁡θσ)≤ϵE1−E0,∀σ∈𝒱ℓ.\psi_{\sigma}^{2}(1-\cos\theta_{\sigma})\leq\frac{\epsilon}{E_{1}-E_{0}},\quad\forall\sigma\in\mathcal{V}_{\ell}.

If ψσ=0\psi_{\sigma}=0 then the inequality is automatically satisfied. For vertices with non-zero amplitudes,

cos⁡θσ≥1−ϵψmin2​(E1−E0),∀ψσ≠0,\cos\theta_{\sigma}\geq 1-\frac{\epsilon}{\psi^{2}_{\mathrm{min}}(E_{1}-E_{0})},\quad\forall\psi_{\sigma}\neq 0,

where ψmin\psi_{\mathrm{min}} is the minimum nonzero amplitude. Combining this result with (69) we find that the following upper bound on ϵ\epsilon is enough to guarantee that GS signs will be reproduced exactly through hyperplane rounding, when the plane is perpendicular to any 𝐯σ\mathbf{v}_{\sigma} for ψσ≠0\psi_{\sigma}\neq 0.

ϵ<(1−cos⁡π4)​ψmin2​(E1−E0).\epsilon<\left(1-\cos\frac{\pi}{4}\right)\psi_{\mathrm{min}}^{2}(E_{1}-E_{0}). (70)

This relation is consistent with our previous assumption, ϵ<E1−E0\epsilon<E_{1}-E_{0}. Now that we know ϵ\epsilon, reaching this accuracy can be done in polynomial time in |𝒱ℓ||\mathcal{V}_{\ell}|. Theorem 3.7 of Ref. [2] shows that solving for XX such that EGW−E0<ϵE_{\textsf{GW}}-E_{0}<\epsilon can be done in 𝒪⁡(|𝒱ℓ|​|ln⁡ϵ|)\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{|\mathcal{V}_{\ell}|}|\ln\epsilon|) steps using interior point method. Each step in interior point requires solving an |𝒱ℓ|×|𝒱ℓ||\mathcal{V}_{\ell}|\times|\mathcal{V}_{\ell}| linear system which costs 𝒪⁡(|𝒱ℓ|3)\mathcal{O}(|\mathcal{V}_{\ell}|^{3}) operations [22], making the total time complexity 𝒪⁡(|𝒱ℓ|3.5​|ln⁡[ψmin2​(E1−E0)]|)\mathcal{O}\left(|\mathcal{V}_{\ell}|^{3.5}|\ln[\psi_{\mathrm{min}}^{2}(E_{1}-E_{0})]|\right). Further estimates can be made by making assumptions about the scaling of the spectral gap E1−E0E_{1}-E_{0} and ψmin\psi_{\mathrm{min}} with the number of spins. In particular, we expect logarithmic corrections in |𝒱ℓ||\mathcal{V}_{\ell}| to the |𝒱ℓ|3.5|\mathcal{V}_{\ell}|^{3.5} scaling when E1−E0E_{1}-E_{0} and ψmin\psi_{\mathrm{min}} decay exponentially with number of spins. The interior point method is only used as a reference in this work, to show that GW algorithm can indeed exactly recover the GS signs in time polynomial in HG size. Table 2 uses the BM factorization due to it being much easier to implement and also due to its efficiency.

We emphasize that this solvability scaling only holds when the weights are generated from GS amplitudes and the scaling is polynomial in |𝒱ℓ||\mathcal{V}_{\ell}|, the HG size, which can be exponential in the number of spins. A lower time complexity may be achieved by exploiting the structure of token graphs, as done in Ref. [65] for unweighted Max-Cut. Nevertheless it is not surprising that GS PRP is exactly solvable in polynomial time in |𝒱ℓ||\mathcal{V}_{\ell}|, since the GS itself can be obtained through exact diagonalization using the Lanczos algorithm in polynomial time [31]. The expression for time complexity states that if the spectral gap E1−E0E_{1}-E_{0} is low or the minimum non-zero amplitude is low then we will need more iterations to solve the signs. A lower spectral gap means it is harder to distinguish the GS from the first excited state, and changing the signs of low-amplitude states creates very little change in energy; thus, more iterations are needed in these cases.

Westerhout et al. [75] used simulated annealing and a greedy algorithm to reconstruct GS signs from GS amplitudes. They found that these methods can reconstruct GS signs extremely accurately on the entire HG and on subgraphs of HG, and the sign reconstruction performs well under perturbation of the GS amplitudes. Moreover, edges with higher-valued weights satisfied PEC more often than edges with lower-valued weights. Based on these observations, they described the resulting sign optimization landscape as non-glassy and very mildly frustrated.

Our results provide a rigorous counterpart to these numerical observations. Solving a general classical Ising model is NP-hard as it is equivalent to solving a general weighted Max-Cut problem. However, we have shown that GS PRP, whose weights are generated from GS amplitudes, is exactly solvable in polynomial time in the number of vertices. The structure imposed on the weights by the GS amplitudes is enough to make the problem tractable. This suggests that the accuracy of simulated annealing and the greedy algorithm when working on the entire HG can also be attributed to the fact that the weights are generated from GS amplitudes and we conjecture that this accuracy should be reproducible on any system described by a real Hamiltonian in a finite-dimensional Hilbert space and with a non-degenerate GS. As for frustration, we have used this term as a topological property of the HG inherited from the physical graph, so our analysis has focused extensively on frustration in unweighted HG. Nevertheless, the Max-Cut picture shows why edges with higher weights should satisfy PEC more often, since maximizing the cut value favors cutting high-weight edges. Two questions lie beyond the scope of this paper and are left for future work: defining an observable to measure the frustration of weighted HG generated from GS amplitudes and how GS PRP behaves on subgraphs of HG, or under perturbation of GS amplitudes.

VI Sign Learning in VMC

In previous sections, we studied the PRP where the weights of the phase-dependent interference terms were determined by fixed amplitudes. We now study the energy minimization of HℓH_{\ell} or equivalently maximization of the Rayleigh quotient of LℓL_{\ell}, the spectral relaxation of Max-Cut on the HG; where amplitudes are allowed to vary. VMC performs this optimization within a chosen ansatz that allows continuous probability amplitudes. But since the HAF GS is real up to a global phase, its sign structure must be well represented by this ansatz. However it has been found that NQS struggle at learning the signs, a binary classification problem, through continuous phase optimization [75, 66, 8]. As such, NQS are often paired with a sign-prior, i.e. associating a pre-defined sign sσs_{\sigma} to each basis |σ⟩\ket{\sigma}, where the prior is a good approximation of the GS signs. Using a particular type of ansatz as an example we now show how continuous optimization of both amplitude and phase leads to a rugged optimization landscape through the inheritance of non-convex features of the Rank-2 relaxation.

VI.1 Optimization Landscape of Complex-valued Ansatz

We follow the standard convention where a variational ansatz parameterizes the logarithm of the probability amplitude instead of the probability amplitude itself [30, Appendix A1]. In this parameterization, the real part of a complex-valued ansatz output gives the logarithm of the wavefunction magnitude, which we call the amplitude, while the imaginary part gives its phase. This ansatz relaxes the signs to continuous phases on a unit circle, which is necessary as discrete signs are not suitable for gradient based methods. When a sign-prior is used, the ansatz only needs to determine the deviation of GS signs from the prior. This sign-prior can be incorporated either into the ansatz as an imaginary number representing the phase or equivalently into the Hamiltonian through a diagonal unitary transformation, which we discuss in details in Sec. VII. We use the former method for convenience.

The amplitude and phase represented by a complex-valued NQS may depend on shared or separate variational parameters [33]. We choose the latter as VMC with this type of ansatz can be shown to have the most direct connection to PRP. We denote the amplitude and phase parameters by the tuples θ\theta and α\alpha, respectively. We also make the deliberate choice of representing the amplitude as ψ⁡(θ)\psi(\theta) instead of eψ⁡(θ)e^{\psi(\theta)}, for notational convenience. The variational ansatz then takes the form,

|Ψθ​α⟩=∑σ∈𝒱ℓψσ​(θ)​ei​ϕσ​(α)​|σ⟩,ψσ>0,ϕσ∈ℝ.\ket{\Psi_{\theta\alpha}}=\sum_{\sigma\in\mathcal{V}_{\ell}}\psi_{\sigma}(\theta)\,e^{i\phi_{\sigma}(\alpha)}\ket{\sigma},\quad\psi_{\sigma}>0,\phi_{\sigma}\in\mathbb{R}.

We work with the untransformed Hamiltonian in ℓ=⌊N/2⌋\ell=\lfloor N/2\rfloor sector and the sign-prior, if used, is accounted for by adding the phase associated with the sign-prior to the imaginary part of the ansatz output. Let

(wℓ)σ​τ​(θ)=2​Hσ​τ​ψσ​(θ)​ψτ​(θ)⟨Ψθ​α|Ψθ​α⟩,∀{σ,τ}∈ℰℓ,(w_{\ell})_{\sigma\tau}\,(\theta)=2\,H_{\sigma\tau}\,\frac{\psi_{\sigma}(\theta)\psi_{\tau}(\theta)}{\braket{\Psi_{\theta\alpha}|\Psi_{\theta\alpha}}},\quad\forall\{\sigma,\tau\}\in\mathcal{E}_{\ell},

be the amplitude-dependent weights, which depend only on θ\theta. The classical and quantum parts of the variational energy then become,

Ec​(θ)\displaystyle E_{c}(\theta) =∑σ∈𝒱ℓψσ​(θ)2​Hσ​σ⟨Ψθ​α|Ψθ​α⟩,\displaystyle=\sum_{\sigma\in\mathcal{V}_{\ell}}\frac{\psi_{\sigma}(\theta)^{2}H_{\sigma\sigma}}{\braket{\Psi_{\theta\alpha}|\Psi_{\theta\alpha}}},
Eq​(θ,α)\displaystyle E_{q}(\theta,\alpha) =∑{σ,τ}∈ℰℓ(wℓ)σ​τ​(θ)​cos⁡[ϕσ​(α)−ϕτ​(α)].\displaystyle=\sum_{\{\sigma,\tau\}\in\mathcal{E}_{\ell}}(w_{\ell})_{\sigma\tau}(\theta)\cos\big[\phi_{\sigma}(\alpha)-\phi_{\tau}(\alpha)\big].

This expression for EqE_{q} differs from Eq. (44) in two ways: the weights are no longer constant, and the phases are also parameterized. The variational energy is the sum of the two parts, E⁡(θ,α)=Ec​(θ)+Eq​(θ,α)E(\theta,\alpha)=E_{c}(\theta)+E_{q}(\theta,\alpha). In VMC, quantities such as the variational energy and its gradient are estimated by averaging local estimators corresponding to the quantities over configurations sampled from the Born distribution [5]. In our case, we only need that VMC provides a stochastic estimate of the variational energy and its gradient. Therefore, we can infer what VMC does by analyzing EcE_{c}, EqE_{q}, and their gradients. Interestingly, the Markov Chain Monte Carlo sampling can be viewed as a random walk on HG with Metropolis–Hastings transition probabilities because magnetization-preserving sampling generates samples using spin exchanges or HFs along the edges of the physical lattice.

When stochastic gradient descent is used, the parameters are updated at every iteration in the opposite direction of the energy gradient. Other gradient-based methods such as stochastic reconfiguration [5] and Adam [29] modify this scheme by transforming the gradient before using it to update the parameters. Analysis of stochastic gradient descent therefore has implications for other methods as well. Now, the phase parameters α\alpha are updated only through derivatives of variational energy with respect to α\alpha itself, i.e. ∇αE\nabla_{\alpha}E, and likewise for θ\theta. Since EcE_{c} is independent of α\alpha, ∇αE=∇αEq\nabla_{\alpha}E=\nabla_{\alpha}E_{q}. So the parameter updates become,

θ←θ−ζ​∇θE​(θ,α),α←α−ζ​∇αEq​(θ,α).\theta\leftarrow\theta-\zeta\,\nabla_{\theta}E(\theta,\alpha),\qquad\alpha\leftarrow\alpha-\zeta\,\nabla_{\alpha}E_{q}(\theta,\alpha).

Here, ζ\zeta is the learning rate. Expanding ∇αEq\nabla_{\alpha}E_{q} gives,

∇αEq=−∑{σ,τ}∈ℰℓ(wℓ)σ​τsin(ϕσ−ϕτ)∇α(ϕσ−ϕτ).\nabla_{\alpha}E_{q}=-\sum_{\{\sigma,\tau\}\in\mathcal{E}_{\ell}}(w_{\ell})_{\sigma\tau}\sin\left(\phi_{\sigma}-\phi_{\tau}\right)\nabla_{\alpha}\left(\phi_{\sigma}-\phi_{\tau}\right). (71)

This is equivalent to Eq. (55) with the phases being parameterized by an ansatz. Thus, at each iteration the phase parameters are updated as if it is solving a PRP on the HG with weights defined by the current θ\theta. That is to say, when amplitude and phase use separate parameters, VMC can be considered as an evolving Rank-2 relaxed Max-Cut problem: The amplitudes and weights evolve during training, and at each step the phases ϕσ​(α)\phi_{\sigma}(\alpha) are updated as in the Rank-2 relaxation method for Max-Cut with weights (wℓ)σ​τ​(θ)(w_{\ell})_{\sigma\tau}\,(\theta) on the HG. Since α\alpha are updated using ∇αE\nabla_{\alpha}E, we need to analyze the optimization landscape of E⁡(θ,α)E(\theta,\alpha) at constant θ\theta to determine the phase learning behavior of the ansatz. Note that this interpretation is only valid when separate parameters are used for phase and amplitude.

The phase ansatz is a map from the parameter space of α\alpha to the space of phases: the ansatz takes the parameters α\alpha and a HG vertex σ\sigma as input and outputs the phase ϕσ​(α)\phi_{\sigma}(\alpha). In the Rank-2 method, the phases ϕσ\phi_{\sigma} are themselves variational parameters, whereas in VMC the phases are parameterized by α\alpha. We now show how continuous parameterization of the phase makes the ansatz inherit the non-convex features of Rank-2 relaxation method, such as the spurious minima and saddle points. We only provide a sketch of the proof; for a rigorous approach, see Proposition 3.6 and Lemma 3.11 of Ref. [34].

Let Φ\Phi be a point in the space of phases with coordinates Φσ\Phi_{\sigma} that is a spurious minimum of the Rank-2 objective, Eq. (54), with weight matrix wℓ​(θ)w_{\ell}(\theta). Let Φ\Phi also be reachable by the ansatz, i.e., let there exist a point αΦ\alpha_{\Phi} in parameter space such that ϕσ​(αΦ)=Φσ\phi_{\sigma}(\alpha_{\Phi})=\Phi_{\sigma} for all σ∈𝒱ℓ\sigma\in\mathcal{V}_{\ell}. Since the ansatz is a continuous map, a small change of parameters, α=αΦ+d​α\alpha=\alpha_{\Phi}+d\alpha, leads to small change of the phases ϕσ​(αΦ+d​α)=Φσ+d​Φ\phi_{\sigma}(\alpha_{\Phi}+d\alpha)=\Phi_{\sigma}+d\Phi. Since Φ\Phi is a local minimum, no point in a sufficiently small neighborhood of Φ\Phi has a lower EqE_{q}. For small enough d​αd\alpha, Φ+d​Φ\Phi+d\Phi lies in this neighborhood, so E⁡(θ,αΦ+d​α)≥E⁡(θ,αΦ)E(\theta,\alpha_{\Phi}+d\alpha)\geq E(\theta,\alpha_{\Phi}). This is true for small deviations in any direction in the parameter space. Hence, αΦ\alpha_{\Phi} is a local minimum of the energy with respect to α\alpha, and if the ansatz can represent energies lower than E⁡(θ,αΦ)E(\theta,\alpha_{\Phi}), it is a spurious minimum. Each minimum is part of a line in the space of phases as shifting every phase by a constant does not affect the energy functional. These lines then become curves in parameter space of α\alpha for continuous mapping.

We now move to saddle points. Continuity alone does not imply that the ansatz is capable of representing two directions in parameter space corresponding to an increase and a decrease in energy. If the ansatz is only continuous but cannot represent both directions, then it may only represent the direction of increase or only the direction of decrease. In that case, the saddle point becomes a spurious minimum or a local maximum. Let Φ\Phi be a saddle point of the Rank-2 objective, Eq. (54). For sufficiently small deviation d​Φd\Phi there exists d​αd\alpha such that ϕσ​(αΦ+d​α)=Φσ+d​Φσ\phi_{\sigma}(\alpha_{\Phi}+d\alpha)=\Phi_{\sigma}+d\Phi_{\sigma}. At a saddle point, there exist at least two directions d​Φ1d\Phi_{1} and d​Φ2d\Phi_{2} such that energy decreases along the first and increases along the second. Under our local expressivity assumption, these two directions have corresponding counterparts d​α1d\alpha_{1} and d​α2d\alpha_{2} in parameter space, respectively. Therefore, E⁡(θ,αΦ+d​α1)<E⁡(θ,αΦ)<E⁡(θ,αΦ+d​α2)E(\theta,\alpha_{\Phi}+d\alpha_{1})<E(\theta,\alpha_{\Phi})<E(\theta,\alpha_{\Phi}+d\alpha_{2}), and (θ,αΦ)(\theta,\alpha_{\Phi}) is a saddle point of energy with respect to α\alpha itself.

As discussed in Sec. V.1, every {0,π}\{0,\pi\} phase assignment, ϕσ∈{0,π}\phi_{\sigma}\in\{0,\pi\} is a stationary point of the Rank-2 objective, Eq. (54) and if the {0,π}\{0,\pi\} assignment does not minimize or maximize the energy globally then it is a saddle point. There are at most 2n−12^{n-1} lines that correspond to such saddle points, where n=|𝒱ℓ|n=|\mathcal{V}_{\ell}|. By Eq. (55) these {0,π}\{0,\pi\} assignments are also stationary points of the phase ansatz. For an expressive ansatz, these lines of saddle points correspond to curves in the parameter space of α\alpha. Since this stationarity does not depend on θ\theta, each line becomes a manifold of dimension |θ|+1|\theta|+1 in the combined parameter space of θ\theta and α\alpha. These manifolds differ from the stationary points that represent energy eigenstates, which form lower-dimensional manifolds in parameter space, as only the global phase and the normalization can be chosen freely.

The image of the phase ansatz in the space of phases is at most |α||\alpha| dimensional and in practice |α|≪|𝒱ℓ||\alpha|\ll|\mathcal{V}_{\ell}|. Therefore the local expressivity only works inside the much lower dimensional image, i.e. points in space of phases exactly representable by the ansatz. The phase ansatz then misses most parts of the lines of {0,π}\{0,\pi\} assignments and only exactly representable minima from Rank-2 objective are inherited. Moreover, the ansatz only sees the Hessian of EqE_{q} with respect to α\alpha, which is not the full picture. The ansatz can at most represent |α||\alpha| independent directions at stationary points which is a small fraction of the |𝒱ℓ||\mathcal{V}_{\ell}| dimensional space. So saddle points whose descent directions are not representable become spurious minima. Let ∇αEq=J⊤​∇ϕEq\nabla_{\alpha}E_{q}=J^{\top}\nabla_{\phi}E_{q}, where J=∂ϕ/∂αJ=\partial\phi/\partial\alpha is the Jacobian and has rank at most |α||\alpha|. So, a point in parameter space, α\alpha, is also stationary whenever ∇ϕEq\nabla_{\phi}E_{q} is orthogonal to the image of JJ, which creates stationary points with no counterpart in the Rank-2 objective, while nearly reachable stationary lines produce plateaus in parameter space. Suffice to say, the optimization landscape remains highly non-convex, consistent with the rugged landscape reported by Bukov et al. [8], who also used separate parameters for amplitude and phase. Our PRP formalism has therefore allowed us to connect the rugged landscape of VMC with the non-convex features of Rank-2 relaxation.

This formalism also allows for a possible explanation of why sign learning is observed to be easier on bipartite lattices [74]. When the physical graph is bipartite the HG is also bipartite and the Max-Cut on HG is therefore independent of the amplitude values, solely determined by the MSR. At each iteration, no matter the value of θ\theta, the MSR globally minimizes Eq​(θ,α)E_{q}(\theta,\alpha). The optimal phases therefore do not move as θ\theta changes. Assuming each update direction on average points towards the current global minima of Eq​(θ,α)E_{q}(\theta,\alpha), for a bipartite lattice α\alpha gets pushed towards the direction of MSR at every iteration. So the sign structure should be learned faster than the non-bipartite case.

VI.2 Interpretation of VMC with Real-valued Ansatz

We now choose a real-valued ansatz which by the convention used, cannot represent the phases and thus the ansatz must be combined with a sign prior. In this case there is no direct relationship with a continuous relaxation of Max-Cut, therefore we will not be able to discuss the optimization landscape as before. However, we can at least show how VMC in this case can be viewed through the lens of HG formulation. Let θ\theta denote the variational parameters, then the variational wavefunction in this case effectively has the following form.

|Ψθ⟩=∑σ∈𝒱ℓsσ​ψσ​(θ)​|σ⟩,ψσ​(θ)>0\ket{\Psi_{\theta}}=\sum_{\sigma\in\mathcal{V}_{\ell}}s_{\sigma}\psi_{\sigma}(\theta)\ket{\sigma},\quad\psi_{\sigma}(\theta)>0

The sign-prior enters the equation through sσs_{\sigma} and ℓ=⌊N/2⌋\ell=\lfloor N/2\rfloor. The definition of parameter dependent weight matrix wℓ​(θ)w_{\ell}(\theta) has the same form as before and so does EcE_{c}. The quantum part of variational energy, however, is different as there are no interference terms.

Eq​(θ)=∑{σ,τ}∈ℰℓ(wℓ)σ​τ​(θ)​sσ​sτE_{q}(\theta)=\sum_{\{\sigma,\tau\}\in\mathcal{E}_{\ell}}(w_{\ell})_{\sigma\tau}(\theta)\,s_{\sigma}s_{\tau}

Here, sσ​sτs_{\sigma}s_{\tau} comes from the sign-prior. Now, a sign-prior defines a sign for each HG vertex and therefore defines a cut in HG. Thus, when a real ansatz is used with a sign prior, VMC optimization works with a pre-defined cut. This realization allows us to see how energy optimization using a real ansatz is constrained by the sign-prior from the HG perspective. The sign prior pre-defines the cut of HG and then VMC has to find the optimal parameters such that the energy is minimized. To get a good approximation of the GS energy the pre-defined cut has to match the Max-Cut formed by GS signs as closely as possible with more priority given to cutting high-weight edges. Therefore getting the signs of states with larger amplitudes right is important. However, for HAF, ignoring special coupling values, correct expressions for the sign-priors are only known when the graph is bipartite. For these cases, PEC is satisfied globally and the Max-Cut is independent of the weights, fixed by the MSR; so no matter the value of the amplitudes, VMC always works with a Max-Cut.

VII Stoquasticity and Max-Cut

In the previous sections, we have studied the sign structure through the phases of the variational wavefunction. We now approach the sign structure from the Hamiltonian side by examining its off-diagonal matrix elements in the computational basis. In the computational basis {|σ⟩}\{\ket{\sigma}\}, a Hamiltonian H^\hat{H} is stoquastic [7] if

⟨σ|H^|τ⟩≤0,for every​σ≠τ.\braket{\sigma|\hat{H}|\tau}\leq 0,\qquad\text{for every}\,\sigma\neq\tau.

We show that a diagonal sign transformation can make HℓH_{\ell} stoquastic when the Max-Cut deficit on coupling-weighted HG vanishes.

The token graph structure of the HG shows the basis dependence for representing the Hamiltonian. In the computational basis, each state specifies the positions of ℓ\ell up spins, which we take as tokens. An HF moves a single token along a physical bond to a site occupied by a down spin. These spin flips establish the isomorphism Γℓ​(G)≅Fℓ​(G)\Gamma_{\ell}(G)\cong F_{\ell}(G). Each HF can therefore be viewed as a token hop between neighboring vertices of the HG, with hopping amplitude Jr/2J_{r}/2 for a physical bond of range rr. The diagonal terms give the energy of the spin configuration at each vertex. In sector ℓ\ell, the HAF Hamiltonian in Eq. (1) takes the form

Hℓ=∑rJr2​∑{σ,τ}∈ℰℓ,r[|σ⟩​⟨τ|+|τ⟩​⟨σ|]+∑σ∈𝒱ℓ[EF−∑rJr2nrap(σ)]|σ⟩⟨σ|.\begin{split}H_{\ell}&=\sum_{r}\frac{J_{r}}{2}\sum_{\{\sigma,\tau\}\in\mathcal{E}_{\ell,r}}\bigg[\ket{\sigma}\bra{\tau}+\ket{\tau}\bra{\sigma}\bigg]\\ &\quad+\sum_{\sigma\in\mathcal{V}_{\ell}}\left[E_{F}-\sum_{r}\frac{J_{r}}{2}n_{r}^{\rm ap}(\sigma)\right]\ket{\sigma}\bra{\sigma}.\end{split} (72)

Equation (72) gives a tight-binding representation of the HAF Hamiltonian on the HG. Here, the hopping term follows from the off-diagonal part of each bond operator Jr​𝐒^i⋅𝐒^jJ_{r}\,\hat{\mathbf{S}}_{i}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{S}}_{j} in GG, which exchanges antiparallel spins on the bond, and nrap​(σ)n_{r}^{\mathrm{ap}}(\sigma) is defined in Eq. (17). In this representation, HℓH_{\ell} is stoquastic if all hopping amplitudes are real and nonpositive, i.e., if every hop has the standard tight-binding form −t-t with t≥0t\geq 0. Since every hopping in Eq. (72) equals +Jr/2>0+J_{r}/2>0, HℓH_{\ell} is not stoquastic in the computational basis. Writing +Jr/2=−(Jr/2)ei​π+J_{r}/2=-(J_{r}/2)\,e^{i\pi} shows that, relative to the standard form, every HG edge carries a Peierls phase π\pi.

We now ask whether a change of basis can remove these Peierls phases. A unitary transformation UℓU_{\ell} that transforms Hℓ→Uℓ​Hℓ​Uℓ†H_{\ell}\to U_{\ell}H_{\ell}U_{\ell}^{\dagger} leaves the spectrum, and hence the GS energy, unchanged, but it can change the on-site energies and hoppings on the HG. For a general UℓU_{\ell}, however, the nonzero off-diagonal elements of Uℓ​Hℓ​Uℓ†U_{\ell}H_{\ell}U_{\ell}^{\dagger} need not correspond to single-token moves along bonds of GG, and the resulting graph need not be isomorphic to Fℓ​(G)F_{\ell}(G).

We first consider a diagonal sign transformation, which preserves the HG connectivity, hopping magnitudes, and onsite energies, and changes only the hopping phases. In sector ℓ\ell, it has the form

Uℓ=∑σ∈𝒱ℓsσ​|σ⟩​⟨σ|,sσ=ei​ϕσ∈{±1}.U_{\ell}=\sum_{\sigma\in\mathcal{V}_{\ell}}s_{\sigma}\ket{\sigma}\bra{\sigma},\quad s_{\sigma}=e^{i\phi_{\sigma}}\in\{\pm 1\}. (73)

Since sσ=±1s_{\sigma}=\pm 1, this unitary satisfies Uℓ†=Uℓ=Uℓ−1U_{\ell}^{\dagger}=U_{\ell}=U_{\ell}^{-1}. It assigns the sign sσs_{\sigma} to each basis state: Uℓ​|σ⟩=sσ​|σ⟩U_{\ell}|\sigma\rangle=s_{\sigma}|\sigma\rangle. Now applying UℓU_{\ell} to HℓH_{\ell} gives

Hℓ′\displaystyle H^{\prime}_{\ell} =Uℓ​Hℓ​Uℓ\displaystyle=U_{\ell}H_{\ell}U_{\ell}
=∑rJr2​∑{σ,τ}∈ℰℓ,rsσ​sτ​[|σ⟩​⟨τ|+|τ⟩​⟨σ|]\displaystyle=\sum_{r}\frac{J_{r}}{2}\sum_{\{\sigma,\tau\}\in\mathcal{E}_{\ell,r}}s_{\sigma}s_{\tau}\bigg[\ket{\sigma}\bra{\tau}+\ket{\tau}\bra{\sigma}\bigg]
+∑σ∈𝒱ℓ[EF−∑rJr2nrap(σ)]|σ⟩⟨σ|.\displaystyle+\sum_{\sigma\in\mathcal{V}_{\ell}}\left[E_{F}-\sum_{r}\frac{J_{r}}{2}n_{r}^{\rm ap}(\sigma)\right]\ket{\sigma}\bra{\sigma}. (74)

Since Jr>0J_{r}>0, the transformed hopping amplitude (Jr/2)​sσ​sτ(J_{r}/2)s_{\sigma}s_{\tau} has the sign of sσ​sτs_{\sigma}s_{\tau}. Thus Hℓ′H_{\ell}^{\prime} is stoquastic if and only if

sσ​sτ=−1for every ​{σ,τ}∈ℰℓ.s_{\sigma}s_{\tau}=-1\qquad\text{for every }\{\sigma,\tau\}\in\mathcal{E}_{\ell}. (75)

In the language of Peierls phases, sσ​sτ=ei⁡(ϕσ−ϕτ)s_{\sigma}s_{\tau}=e^{i(\phi_{\sigma}-\phi_{\tau})}, so UℓU_{\ell} adds the phase difference ϕσ−ϕτ\phi_{\sigma}-\phi_{\tau} (equal to π\pi on PEC edges and 00 on ZEC edges) to the phase π\pi on each edge, and Eq. (75) requires this difference to cancel the π\pi on every edge. This edgewise cancellation is equivalent to the cycle condition of Ref. [24], specialized to the HAF, where every hop carries the same phase. Following Theorem 4, this is possible only when the physical lattice is bipartite, and the diagonal unitary can then be chosen explicitly as the Lieb–Mattis operator [36, 37]

η=(−1)NA↑=(−1)|A|​∏i∈VAσiz.\eta=(-1)^{N_{A}^{\uparrow}}=(-1)^{|A|}\prod_{i\in V_{A}}\sigma_{i}^{z}.

Here the bipartite physical graph is G=(VA⊔VB,E)G=(V_{A}\sqcup V_{B},E) with disjoint sublattices VAV_{A} and VBV_{B}, and N^A↑=∑i∈VA12​(I+σ^iz)\hat{N}^{\uparrow}_{A}=\sum_{i\in V_{A}}\tfrac{1}{2}(I+\hat{\sigma}^{z}_{i}) counts the number of up-spins on VAV_{A} (35). Restricted to sector ℓ\ell, η^\hat{\eta} is the unitary UℓU_{\ell} in Eq. (73) that makes the bipartite-graph Hamiltonian stoquastic.

η​|σ⟩=(−1)NA↑​(σ)​|σ⟩={+|σ⟩,NA↑​(σ)​even,−|σ⟩,NA↑​(σ)​odd.\eta\ket{\sigma}=(-1)^{N_{A}^{\uparrow}(\sigma)}\ket{\sigma}=\begin{cases}+\ket{\sigma},&N_{A}^{\uparrow}(\sigma)\ \text{even},\\ -\ket{\sigma},&N_{A}^{\uparrow}(\sigma)\ \text{odd}.\end{cases} (76)

Comparing Eq. (76) with Uℓ​|σ⟩=sσ​|σ⟩U_{\ell}|\sigma\rangle=s_{\sigma}|\sigma\rangle gives

sσ=(−1)NA↑​(σ),ϕσ=π​NA↑​(σ),s_{\sigma}=(-1)^{N_{A}^{\uparrow}(\sigma)},\qquad\phi_{\sigma}=\pi N_{A}^{\uparrow}(\sigma),

which is the Marshall sign in Eq. (36) and the PEC Eq. (46). On a bipartite lattice, every HF changes NA↑N_{A}^{\uparrow} by one. The LM signs therefore differ across every HG edge, giving a cut that contains all edges and is a Max-Cut for any nonnegative edge weights (Fig. 3). The same sign assignment makes every hopping amplitude negative, so the transformed Hamiltonian Hℓ′=η​Hℓ​ηH_{\ell}^{\prime}=\eta H_{\ell}\eta is stoquastic.

On a non-bipartite lattice, however, no binary sign assignment can cut every HG edge. The cut edges satisfy the PEC condition, while the uncut edges satisfy the ZEC given by

ℰPEC\displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{PEC}} ={{σ,τ}∈ℰℓ|sσ​sτ=−1},\displaystyle=\bigl\{\{\sigma,\tau\}\in\mathcal{E}_{\ell}\,\big|\,s_{\sigma}s_{\tau}=-1\bigr\},
ℰZEC\displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{ZEC}} ={{σ,τ}∈ℰℓ|sσ​sτ=+1}.\displaystyle=\bigl\{\{\sigma,\tau\}\in\mathcal{E}_{\ell}\,\big|\,s_{\sigma}s_{\tau}=+1\bigr\}.

Consequently the Max-Cut value for coupling-weighted adjacency decreases from the upper bound (Wℓ)tot=∑{σ,τ}∈ℰℓ(Wℓ)σ​τ(W_{\ell})_{\mathrm{tot}}=\sum_{\{\sigma,\tau\}\in\mathcal{E}_{\ell}}(W_{\ell})_{\sigma\tau}. The off-diagonal elements that remain positive represent ZEC edges in HG. A measure of these residual positive off-diagonal weights is

R⁡(Uℓ)=∑{σ,τ}∈ℰZEC(Wℓ)σ​τ=(Wℓ)tot−CutWℓ​(s).R(U_{\ell})=\sum_{\{\sigma,\tau\}\in\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{ZEC}}}(W_{\ell})_{\sigma\tau}=(W_{\ell})_{\mathrm{tot}}-\mathrm{Cut}_{W_{\ell}}(s).

We call this the cut deficiency. Then,

min⁡R⁡(Uℓ)=(Wℓ)tot−Max-Cut​(Wℓ)\min R(U_{\ell})=(W_{\ell})_{\mathrm{tot}}-\textsf{Max-Cut}(W_{\ell})

is the Max-Cut deficiency. The following theorem follows from this definition.

Theorem 6.

A diagonal real unitary transformation UℓU_{\ell} that can make Hℓ′=Uℓ​Hℓ​UℓH_{\ell}^{\prime}=U_{\ell}H_{\ell}U_{\ell} stoquastic exists if and only if the Max-Cut deficiency min⁡R⁡(Uℓ)=0\min R(U_{\ell})=0.

Proof.

The transformed Hamiltonian Hℓ′H_{\ell}^{\prime} is stoquastic when all off-diagonal elements are non-positive. Hence sσ​sτ=−1s_{\sigma}s_{\tau}=-1 on every edge and PEC is obeyed globally. Thus, no edge satisfies the ZEC conditions and the MSR gives R⁡(Uℓ)=0R(U_{\ell})=0, which is also the minimum of R⁡(Uℓ)R(U_{\ell}) as the weights are non-negative. Conversely, when there exists a sign assignment sσs_{\sigma} such that R⁡(Uℓ)=0R(U_{\ell})=0 then due to all (Wℓ)σ​τ(W_{\ell})_{\sigma\tau} being non-negative for HAF, we get global PEC which implies Hℓ′H_{\ell}^{\prime} is stoquastic. ∎

By the Perron-Frobenius theorem, when a unitary transformation renders the Hamiltonian stoquastic, the GS becomes positive, i.e., all signs of the GS probability amplitudes can be chosen to be +1+1. Thereby, R⁡(Uℓ)=0R(U_{\ell})=0 implies a positive ground state. However, deviation of R⁡(Uℓ)R(U_{\ell}) from zero is not guaranteed to break this positivity, even though it breaks the stoquasticity.

In J1J_{1}–J2J_{2} models, the exact LM transformation can still survive at special coupling limits. For example, in the square-lattice J1J_{1}–J2J_{2} HAF, G=(V,E1)G=(V,E_{1}) at J2=0J_{2}=0 and G=(V,E2)G=(V,E_{2}) at J1=0J_{1}=0; at both limits the physical graph is bipartite. Assuming the probability amplitudes vary continuously with J2/J1J_{2}/J_{1}, it is reasonable to expect the sign structure at a particular J2/J1J_{2}/J_{1} to persist near that coupling and the signs of the states with larger amplitudes should persist longer. In terms of Max-Cut, we can argue that the weights also change continuously, hence the Max-Cut at a coupling value should work as a very accurate estimation of the Max-Cut for neighboring couplings as well. Therefore near each of these limits the canonical LM parity operator, η\eta provides a natural sign prior, where VAV_{A} is a disjoint sublattice of (V,E1)(V,E_{1}) for J2≪J1J_{2}\ll J_{1} and disjoint sublattice of (V,E2)(V,E_{2}) for J2≫J1J_{2}\gg J_{1} [14]. Due to the anticommutation of Pauli operators, the Hamiltonian is transformed as,

H^′=∑r=12Jr​∑{i,j}∈Er[S^iz​S^jz+vi​vj​(S^ix​S^jx+S^iy​S^jy)],\hat{H}^{\prime}=\sum_{r=1}^{2}J_{r}\sum_{\{i,j\}\in E_{r}}\left[\hat{S}^{z}_{i}\hat{S}^{z}_{j}+v_{i}v_{j}\left(\hat{S}^{x}_{i}\hat{S}^{x}_{j}+\hat{S}^{y}_{i}\hat{S}^{y}_{j}\right)\right], (77)

where vi=−1v_{i}=-1 whenever i∈Ai\in A, otherwise vi=+1v_{i}=+1. Eq. (77) and Eq. (74) are related by HFs.

sσ​sτ=vi​vj,∀σ​⇌i​j​τ.s_{\sigma}s_{\tau}=v_{i}v_{j},\quad\forall\,\sigma\overset{ij}{\rightleftharpoons}\tau.

The transformation shows that for any nonzero finite J2/J1J_{2}/J_{1}, some off-diagonal elements remain positive, breaking stoquasticity even though we can argue perturbatively that the GS remains positive in special limits. Beyond such special cases, however, no analogous a priori grading determined solely by the lattice structure is generally available. Nevertheless, this discussion contrasts the quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) sign problem [59, 51] with the VMC sign learning problem. Solving the QMC sign problem always solves the VMC sign-learning problem if the ansatz takes the rotated basis states as input. But solving the VMC sign-learning problem only requires a transformation that maps the GS to a positive vector, which may not make the Hamiltonian stoquastic.

The diagonal unitary transformations considered here preserve the HG connectivity, and hence its token-graph structure, while changing only the phases of the off-diagonal Hamiltonian matrix elements. From this viewpoint, searching for a stoquastic representation means constructing a new weighted HG for the unitarily transformed Hamiltonian, with real, nonpositive off-diagonal matrix elements. The resulting HG need not retain the token-graph structure. The problem is therefore to find efficiently constructible non-diagonal transformations that produce a non-token stoquastic HG at fixed system size and magnetization, while keeping the transformed Hamiltonian efficiently representable. This connects our graph perspective to the broader search for stoquastic bases studied by Marvian et al. [42]. We leave these transformations and the structure of the resulting HGs for future work.

VIII Average Sign and Estrada bipartivity

In this work, we have studied the sign-learning difficulty of NQS in VMC from the HG viewpoint and used Estrada’s bipartivity index in Subsec. III.3 to quantify the HG’s departure from bipartiteness. The even and odd closed walks underlying this index also determine the average sign in QMC. For the HAF, we derive an exact relation between the average sign and a temperature-dependent generalization of Estrada’s index that retains the Hamiltonian’s diagonal contributions.

Using the Hamiltonian–Laplacian identity in Eq. (23), the sector Hamiltonian is Hℓ=EF​I−LℓH_{\ell}=E_{F}I-L_{\ell}, where Lℓ=Dℓ−WℓL_{\ell}=D_{\ell}-W_{\ell} as defined in Eq. (22). Here, WℓW_{\ell} is the coupling-weighted adjacency matrix and DℓD_{\ell} is its weighted degree matrix in Eq. (18). Replacing every off-diagonal element of HℓH_{\ell} by minus its absolute value changes WℓW_{\ell} to −Wℓ-W_{\ell}. The stoquastic partner is therefore

Hℓ,sq=EF−Qℓ,Qℓ=Dℓ+Wℓ,H_{\ell,\mathrm{sq}}=E_{F}-Q_{\ell},\qquad Q_{\ell}=D_{\ell}+W_{\ell}, (78)

where QℓQ_{\ell} is obtained by removing signs from the Laplacian. The average sign, ⟨s⟩ℓ,β\braket{s}_{\ell,\beta}, is the ratio of the partition function of HAF Hamiltonian, Tr⁡(e−β​Hℓ)\operatorname{Tr}(e^{-\beta H_{\ell}}) and the partition function of its stoquastic partner, Tr⁡(e−β​Hℓ,sq)\operatorname{Tr}(e^{-\beta H_{\ell,\mathrm{sq}}}) [51]. The constant EFE_{F} contributes the same factor e−β​EFe^{-\beta E_{F}} to both partition functions and cancels in the ratio. In terms of LℓL_{\ell} and QℓQ_{\ell}, the average sign ⟨s⟩ℓ,β\langle s\rangle_{\ell,\beta} is given by

⟨s⟩ℓ,β=Tr⁡[eβ​Lℓ]Tr⁡[eβ​Qℓ]=Tr⁡[eβ⁡(Dℓ−Wℓ)]Tr⁡[eβ⁡(Dℓ+Wℓ)].\langle s\rangle_{\ell,\beta}=\frac{\mathrm{Tr}\left[e^{\beta L_{\ell}}\right]}{\mathrm{Tr}\left[e^{\beta Q_{\ell}}\right]}=\frac{\mathrm{Tr}\left[e^{\beta(D_{\ell}-W_{\ell})}\right]}{\mathrm{Tr}\left[e^{\beta(D_{\ell}+W_{\ell})}\right]}. (79)

To separate the closed sequences according to their number of HG hops, we expand the exponentials in Eq. (79):

Tr⁡[eβ⁡(Dℓ±Wℓ)]=∑n=0∞βnn!​Tr​[(Dℓ±Wℓ)n].\mathrm{Tr}\left[e^{\beta(D_{\ell}\pm W_{\ell})}\right]=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{\beta^{n}}{n!}\mathrm{Tr}\left[(D_{\ell}\pm W_{\ell})^{n}\right].

At order nn, distributing the factors produces ordered products, which we call operator words,

𝕎ℓ=X1X2⋯Xn,Xj∈{Dℓ,Wℓ}.\mathbb{W}_{\ell}=X_{1}X_{2}\cdots X_{n},\qquad X_{j}\in\{D_{\ell},W_{\ell}\}.

Let 𝒲n\mathscr{W}_{n} denote the set of these words, and NW​(𝕎ℓ)N_{W}(\mathbb{W}_{\ell}) the number of WℓW_{\ell} factors in 𝕎ℓ\mathbb{W}_{\ell}. Each word appears with a factor (−1)NW​(𝕎ℓ)(-1)^{N_{W}(\mathbb{W}_{\ell})} in the expansion of (Dℓ−Wℓ)n(D_{\ell}-W_{\ell})^{n}, while every word has a positive coefficient in (Dℓ+Wℓ)n(D_{\ell}+W_{\ell})^{n}. Hence, we can write

Tr​𝕎ℓ=∑σ0,…,σn−1∏j=1n(Xj)σj−1​σj,σn=σ0.\mathrm{Tr}\,\mathbb{W}_{\ell}=\sum_{\sigma_{0},\ldots,\sigma_{n-1}}\prod_{j=1}^{n}(X_{j})_{\sigma_{j-1}\sigma_{j}},\qquad\sigma_{n}=\sigma_{0}.

The trace therefore forces each contributing sequence to return to its starting HG vertex. Since DℓD_{\ell} is the diagonal degree matrix, a factor of DℓD_{\ell} leaves the configuration unchanged and contributes the weighted degree Dσ​σD_{\sigma\sigma}. An WℓW_{\ell} factor moves between adjacent configurations in HG and contributes the edge weight (Wℓ)σ​τ(W_{\ell})_{\sigma\tau}. By Eq. (16), this weight is Jr/2J_{r}/2 for {σ,τ}∈ℰℓ,r\{\sigma,\tau\}\in\mathcal{E}_{\ell,r}. Thus, every contributing sequence in Tr​𝕎\mathrm{Tr}\,\mathbb{W} contains exactly NW​(𝕎ℓ)N_{W}(\mathbb{W}_{\ell}) hops.

We classify a closed sequence as even or odd according to this hopping number. Diagonal stays do not affect its parity. For example, Dℓ3D_{\ell}^{3} and Dℓ​Wℓ2D_{\ell}W_{\ell}^{2} belong to the even sector, whereas Dℓ​Wℓ3D_{\ell}W_{\ell}^{3} belongs to the odd sector despite appearing at fourth order in β\beta. We now define the total weights of the two sectors:

Eℓ​(β)\displaystyle E_{\ell}(\beta) =∑n=0∞βnn!​∑𝕎ℓ∈𝒲nNW​(𝕎ℓ)​evenTr⁡𝕎ℓ,\displaystyle=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{\beta^{n}}{n!}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbb{W}_{\ell}\in\mathscr{W}_{n}\\ N_{W}(\mathbb{W}_{\ell})\ \mathrm{even}\end{subarray}}\operatorname{Tr}\mathbb{W}_{\ell},
Oℓ​(β)\displaystyle O_{\ell}(\beta) =∑n=0∞βnn!​∑𝕎ℓ∈𝒲nNW​(𝕎ℓ)​oddTr⁡𝕎ℓ.\displaystyle=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{\beta^{n}}{n!}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbb{W}_{\ell}\in\mathscr{W}_{n}\\ N_{W}(\mathbb{W}_{\ell})\ \mathrm{odd}\end{subarray}}\operatorname{Tr}\mathbb{W}_{\ell}.

All contributions to these sums are nonnegative for β≥0\beta\geq 0. The empty word at n=0n=0 is the identity and belongs to the even sector, giving Eℓ​(0)=|𝒱ℓ|E_{\ell}(0)=|\mathcal{V}_{\ell}| and Oℓ​(0)=0O_{\ell}(0)=0. Consequently,

Tr⁡[eβ​Lℓ]\displaystyle\operatorname{Tr}\left[e^{\beta L_{\ell}}\right] =Eℓ​(β)−Oℓ​(β),\displaystyle=E_{\ell}(\beta)-O_{\ell}(\beta),
Tr⁡[eβ​Qℓ]\displaystyle\operatorname{Tr}\left[e^{\beta Q_{\ell}}\right] =Eℓ​(β)+Oℓ​(β).\displaystyle=E_{\ell}(\beta)+O_{\ell}(\beta).

This even and odd decomposition is the same one that underlies Estrada’s spectral bipartivity [18], introduced in Sec. III.3 and denoted there by β\beta. Since we now use β\beta to denote the inverse temperature, we do not use that symbol for the Estrada index. Instead, we define a temperature-dependent generalization that includes the diagonal stays,

ℬℓ​(β)=Eℓ​(β)Eℓ​(β)+Oℓ​(β).\mathcal{B}_{\ell}(\beta)=\frac{E_{\ell}(\beta)}{E_{\ell}(\beta)+O_{\ell}(\beta)}. (80)

This generalized Estrada bipartivity index measures the fraction of the total absolute weight carried by closed sequences with an even number of hops. Substituting into Eq. (79), we obtain

⟨s⟩ℓ,β=Eℓ​(β)−Oℓ​(β)Eℓ​(β)+Oℓ​(β)=2​ℬℓ​(β)−1.\langle s\rangle_{\ell,\beta}=\frac{E_{\ell}(\beta)-O_{\ell}(\beta)}{E_{\ell}(\beta)+O_{\ell}(\beta)}=2\mathcal{B}_{\ell}(\beta)-1. (81)

The relation is exact and retains the full contribution of the degree matrix DℓD_{\ell}.

For a finite HG and a finite inverse temperature β≥0\beta\geq 0, the nonnegative walk weights imply the following.

Theorem 7.

Let Γℓ\Gamma_{\ell} be a finite, undirected HG with nonnegative edge weights, coupling weighted adjacency matrix WℓW_{\ell} and degree matrix DℓD_{\ell}. Let Eℓ​(β)E_{\ell}(\beta) and Oℓ​(β)O_{\ell}(\beta) denote the even and odd hopping weights defined above. Then, for every finite β≥0\beta\geq 0, the ratio

Rℓ​(β)=Oℓ​(β)Eℓ​(β).R_{\ell}(\beta)=\frac{O_{\ell}(\beta)}{E_{\ell}(\beta)}.

is well-defined and satisfies

0≤Rℓ​(β)<10\leq R_{\ell}(\beta)<1 (82)
Proof.

Since Γℓ\Gamma_{\ell} is finite, DℓD_{\ell} and WℓW_{\ell} are finite matrices with nonnegative entries. Every contribution of Eℓ​(β)E_{\ell}(\beta) and Oℓ​(β)O_{\ell}(\beta) is therefore nonnegative for β≥0\beta\geq 0, and both series converge because their sum is Eℓ​(β)+Oℓ​(β)=Tr⁡[eβ​Qℓ]∈ℝE_{\ell}(\beta)+O_{\ell}(\beta)=\mathrm{Tr}\,[e^{\beta Q_{\ell}}]\in\mathbb{R}. The empty operator word belongs to the even sector and contributes Tr​I=|𝒱ℓ|>0\mathrm{Tr}\,I=|\mathcal{V}_{\ell}|>0. Therefore

Eℓ​(β)≥|𝒱ℓ|>0,Oℓ​(β)≥0.E_{\ell}(\beta)\geq|\mathcal{V}_{\ell}|>0,\qquad O_{\ell}(\beta)\geq 0.

Moreover, writing Lℓ=Dℓ−WℓL_{\ell}=D_{\ell}-W_{\ell}, the even–odd decomposition gives

Eℓ​(β)−Oℓ​(β)=Tr⁡[eβ​Lℓ]=∑j=1|𝒱ℓ|eβ​λj​(Lℓ)>0,E_{\ell}(\beta)-O_{\ell}(\beta)=\mathrm{Tr}\left[e^{\beta L_{\ell}}\right]=\sum_{j=1}^{|\mathcal{V}_{\ell}|}e^{\beta\lambda_{j}(L_{\ell})}>0,

where λj​(Lℓ)\lambda_{j}(L_{\ell}) are the real non-negative eigenvalues of the symmetric positive semi-definite matrix LℓL_{\ell}. Thus 0≤Oℓ​(β)<Eℓ​(β)0\leq O_{\ell}(\beta)<E_{\ell}(\beta). Dividing by Eℓ​(β)>0E_{\ell}(\beta)>0 proves the result. ∎

In terms of Rℓ​(β)R_{\ell}(\beta), the average sign in Eq. (81) and generalized bipartivity in Eq. (80) take the forms

⟨s⟩ℓ,β=1−Rℓ​(β)1+Rℓ​(β),ℬℓ​(β)=11+Rℓ​(β).\langle s\rangle_{\ell,\beta}=\frac{1-R_{\ell}(\beta)}{1+R_{\ell}(\beta)},\qquad\mathcal{B}_{\ell}(\beta)=\frac{1}{1+R_{\ell}(\beta)}. (83)

Their bounds follow immediately:

12<ℬℓ​(β)≤1,0<⟨s⟩ℓ,β≤1.\frac{1}{2}<\mathcal{B}_{\ell}(\beta)\leq 1,\qquad 0<\langle s\rangle_{\ell,\beta}\leq 1. (84)

The upper bound is reached when Oℓ​(β)=0O_{\ell}(\beta)=0, so all contributing closed sequences have an even number of hops. As the odd-sector weight approaches the even-sector weight, ℬℓ​(β)\mathcal{B}_{\ell}(\beta) approaches 1/21/2 and the average sign approaches zero. The same dynamics is responsible for the bounds in Estrada bipartivity (39).

For β>0\beta>0, the upper bound characterizes bipartiteness of the HG. If the HG is bipartite, every closed walk contains an even number of hops. Diagonal stays preserve this parity, so Oℓ​(β)=0O_{\ell}(\beta)=0 and the average sign is unity at every temperature. Conversely, if the HG contains an odd cycle of length gg, then Tr⁡(Wℓg)>0\operatorname{Tr}(W_{\ell}^{g})>0. The corresponding term

βgg!​Tr⁡(Wℓg)\frac{\beta^{g}}{g!}\operatorname{Tr}(W_{\ell}^{g})

makes a strictly positive contribution to Oℓ​(β)O_{\ell}(\beta) for every β>0\beta>0. Therefore,

ℬℓ(β)=1⟺Γℓ(G) is bipartite,∀β>0.\mathcal{B}_{\ell}(\beta)=1\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\Gamma_{\ell}(G)\text{ is bipartite},\quad\forall\beta>0. (85)

Thus, the average sign being unity also implies the HG is bipartite. The restriction β>0\beta>0 is essential: at β=0\beta=0, only the empty word contributes, giving ℬℓ​(0)=1\mathcal{B}_{\ell}(0)=1 for every HG. In the high-temperature limit, β→0\beta\to 0 and since Eℓ​(0)=|𝒱ℓ|E_{\ell}(0)=|\mathcal{V}_{\ell}| and Oℓ​(0)=0O_{\ell}(0)=0,

limβ→0ℬℓ​(β)=1,limβ→0⟨s⟩ℓ,β=1.\lim_{\beta\to 0}\mathcal{B}_{\ell}(\beta)=1,\qquad\lim_{\beta\to 0}\langle s\rangle_{\ell,\beta}=1.

This limit holds for every HG, including nonbipartite graphs: the factors βn→0\beta^{n}\to 0 suppress all contributions containing hops.

To determine the leading order term in the expansion of average sign in terms of β\beta, we recall that WℓW_{\ell} is off-diagonal. A sequence containing only one hop cannot close, regardless of how many diagonal stays it contains. The first possible odd contribution therefore comes from three-hop closed walks:

Oℓ​(β)=β36​Tr⁡(Wℓ3)+𝒪⁡(β4).O_{\ell}(\beta)=\frac{\beta^{3}}{6}\operatorname{Tr}(W_{\ell}^{3})+\mathcal{O}(\beta^{4}).

Using Eℓ​(β)=|𝒱ℓ|+𝒪⁡(β)E_{\ell}(\beta)=|\mathcal{V}_{\ell}|+\mathcal{O}(\beta), we obtain

ℬℓ​(β)=1−Tr⁡(Wℓ3)6​|𝒱ℓ|​β3+𝒪⁡(β4).\mathcal{B}_{\ell}(\beta)=1-\frac{\operatorname{Tr}(W_{\ell}^{3})}{6|\mathcal{V}_{\ell}|}\beta^{3}+\mathcal{O}(\beta^{4}). (86)

The average sign then becomes,

⟨s⟩ℓ,β=1−β33​|𝒱ℓ|​Tr⁡(Wℓ3)+𝒪⁡(β4).\langle s\rangle_{\ell,\beta}=1-\frac{\beta^{3}}{3|\mathcal{V}_{\ell}|}\operatorname{Tr}\left(W_{\ell}^{3}\right)+\mathcal{O}(\beta^{4}). (87)

The trace in Eq. (87) sums the weights of closed walks of three hops on the HG. Each such walk traverses a triangle, giving

Tr⁡(Wℓ3)=6​∑{σ,τ,ρ}∈𝒯ℓ(Wℓ)σ​τ​(Wℓ)τ​ρ​(Wℓ)ρ​σ.\operatorname{Tr}(W_{\ell}^{3})=6\sum_{\{\sigma,\tau,\rho\}\in\mathcal{T}_{\ell}}(W_{\ell})_{\sigma\tau}(W_{\ell})_{\tau\rho}(W_{\ell})_{\rho\sigma}. (88)

Here 𝒯ℓ\mathcal{T}_{\ell} is the set of HG triangles, each counted once, with |𝒯ℓ|=N△​(Γℓ)|\mathcal{T}_{\ell}|=N_{\triangle}(\Gamma_{\ell}) as defined in Eq. (37). Recalling Wℓ=J12​Aℓ,1+J22​Aℓ,2W_{\ell}=\frac{J_{1}}{2}A_{\ell,1}+\frac{J_{2}}{2}A_{\ell,2} from Eq. (16), each matrix element contributes Jr/2J_{r}/2 for a range-rr edge. Thus, Eq. (88) weights each triangle by the product of its three edge weights. The factor of six accounts for three starting vertices and two traversal directions. Thus, the leading possible reduction of the average sign is determined by the total weighted triangle contribution per HG vertex. If the HG contains no triangles, this cubic term vanishes.

To calculate the higher-order corrections, we use the odd-to-even ratio Rℓ​(β)R_{\ell}(\beta) defined in Theorem 7.

Eℓ​(β)=∑n=0∞en​βn,Oℓ​(β)=∑n=0∞on​βn,Rℓ​(β)=∑n=0∞rn​βn.E_{\ell}(\beta)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}e_{n}\beta^{n},\,\,O_{\ell}(\beta)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}o_{n}\beta^{n},\,\,R_{\ell}(\beta)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}r_{n}\beta^{n}.

Here, ene_{n} and ono_{n} collect the traces of operator words with an even or odd number of WℓW_{\ell} factors, respectively, including the factor 1/n!1/n!. Substituting these series into the identity Oℓ​(β)=Rℓ​(β)​Eℓ​(β)O_{\ell}(\beta)=R_{\ell}(\beta)E_{\ell}(\beta) and equating coefficients of the same power of β\beta gives

on=∑k=0nek​rn−k.o_{n}=\sum_{k=0}^{n}e_{k}r_{n-k}.

Since e0=|𝒱ℓ|e_{0}=|\mathcal{V}_{\ell}|, the coefficients can be determined recursively:

r0=o0|𝒱ℓ|,rn=1|𝒱ℓ|​(on−∑k=1nek​rn−k),n≥1r_{0}=\frac{o_{0}}{|\mathcal{V}_{\ell}|},\qquad r_{n}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{V}_{\ell}|}\left(o_{n}-\sum_{k=1}^{n}e_{k}r_{n-k}\right),\qquad n\geq 1

For the loopless HG, o0=o1=o2=0o_{0}=o_{1}=o_{2}=0, and hence r0=r1=r2=0r_{0}=r_{1}=r_{2}=0. Through fifth order, the ratio therefore takes the form

Rℓ​(β)=r3​β3+r4​β4+r5​β5+𝒪⁡(β6)R_{\ell}(\beta)=r_{3}\beta^{3}+r_{4}\beta^{4}+r_{5}\beta^{5}+\mathcal{O}(\beta^{6})

Using the exact relation between this ratio and the average sign,

⟨s⟩ℓ,β=1−Rℓ​(β)1+Rℓ​(β)=1−2​Rℓ​(β)+2​Rℓ​(β)2+𝒪⁡(Rℓ​(β)3)\langle s\rangle_{\ell,\beta}=\frac{1-R_{\ell}(\beta)}{1+R_{\ell}(\beta)}=1-2R_{\ell}(\beta)+2R_{\ell}(\beta)^{2}+\mathcal{O}(R_{\ell}(\beta)^{3})

we obtain

⟨s⟩ℓ,β=1−2​r3​β3−2​r4​β4−2​r5​β5+𝒪⁡(β6),\langle s\rangle_{\ell,\beta}=1-2r_{3}\beta^{3}-2r_{4}\beta^{4}-2r_{5}\beta^{5}+\mathcal{O}(\beta^{6}),

where

r4\displaystyle r_{4} =Tr⁡(Dℓ​Wℓ3)6​|𝒱ℓ|−Tr⁡(Dℓ)​Tr⁡(Wℓ3)6​|𝒱ℓ|2,\displaystyle=\frac{\operatorname{Tr}(D_{\ell}W_{\ell}^{3})}{6|\mathcal{V}_{\ell}|}-\frac{\operatorname{Tr}(D_{\ell})\operatorname{Tr}(W_{\ell}^{3})}{6|\mathcal{V}_{\ell}|^{2}},
r5\displaystyle r_{5} =Tr⁡(Dℓ2​Wℓ3)+Tr⁡(Dℓ​Wℓ​Dℓ​Wℓ2)24​|𝒱ℓ|+Tr⁡(Wℓ5)120​|𝒱ℓ|\displaystyle=\frac{\operatorname{Tr}(D_{\ell}^{2}W_{\ell}^{3})+\operatorname{Tr}(D_{\ell}W_{\ell}D_{\ell}W_{\ell}^{2})}{24|\mathcal{V}_{\ell}|}+\frac{\operatorname{Tr}(W_{\ell}^{5})}{120|\mathcal{V}_{\ell}|}
−Tr⁡(Dℓ)​Tr⁡(Dℓ​Wℓ3)6​|𝒱ℓ|2+[Tr⁡(Dℓ)]2​Tr⁡(Wℓ3)6​|𝒱ℓ|3\displaystyle-\frac{\operatorname{Tr}(D_{\ell})\operatorname{Tr}(D_{\ell}W_{\ell}^{3})}{6|\mathcal{V}_{\ell}|^{2}}+\frac{[\operatorname{Tr}(D_{\ell})]^{2}\operatorname{Tr}(W_{\ell}^{3})}{6|\mathcal{V}_{\ell}|^{3}}
−[Tr⁡(Dℓ2)+Tr⁡(Wℓ2)]​Tr⁡(Wℓ3)12​|𝒱ℓ|2.\displaystyle-\frac{\left[\operatorname{Tr}(D_{\ell}^{2})+\operatorname{Tr}(W_{\ell}^{2})\right]\operatorname{Tr}(W_{\ell}^{3})}{12|\mathcal{V}_{\ell}|^{2}}.

Fig. 6 shows a diagrammatic representation of odd closed walks contributing to the ratio Rℓ​(β)R_{\ell}(\beta). In Ref. [24], Hen relates QMC configuration signs to closed-walk phases on the Hamiltonian graph. Here, we connect the average sign to generalized Estrada bipartivity while retaining diagonal contributions.

The higher-order corrections contain both longer odd closed walks and diagonal stays along shorter walks. At fourth order, the odd sector contains triangular walks with one stay. At fifth order, it contains five-hop closed walks and triangular walks with two stays. The trace Tr⁡(W5)\mathrm{Tr}\left(W^{5}\right) includes simple five-cycles as well as walks that traverse a triangle and retrace an edge. The mixed traces involving DℓD_{\ell} weight the triangular walks according to the vertices at which the stays occur.

Each diagonal stay increases the order in β\beta without changing the hopping parity. Normalization by Eℓ​(β)E_{\ell}(\beta) also introduces products of traces, such as Tr⁡(W2)​Tr​(W3)\mathrm{Tr}\left(W^{2}\right)\mathrm{Tr}\left(W^{3}\right). Although such products do not represent a single closed walk, they retain an odd total number of WℓW_{\ell} factors. Thus, the coefficients r4r_{4} and r5r_{5} incorporate both the odd-walk weights and their normalization by the even-sector weight.

Finally, the generalized bipartivity reduces to Estrada’s adjacency-based expression when the diagonal part of the Hamiltonian is constant. For the HAF, this occurs when the HG has constant weighted degree, Dℓ=dℓ​ID_{\ell}=d_{\ell}I. In this case,

Tr⁡eβ⁡(Dℓ±Wℓ)=eβ​dℓ​Tr⁡e±β​Wℓ.\operatorname{Tr}e^{\beta(D_{\ell}\pm W_{\ell})}=e^{\beta d_{\ell}}\operatorname{Tr}e^{\pm\beta W_{\ell}}.

The common factor cancels in the average sign, giving

⟨s⟩ℓ,β=Tr⁡e−β​WℓTr⁡eβ​Wℓ.\langle s\rangle_{\ell,\beta}=\frac{\operatorname{Tr}e^{-\beta W_{\ell}}}{\operatorname{Tr}e^{\beta W_{\ell}}}.

Using ℬℓ​(β)=12​(1+⟨s⟩ℓ,β)\mathcal{B}_{\ell}(\beta)=\tfrac{1}{2}(1+\langle s\rangle_{\ell,\beta}), we obtain

ℬℓ​(β)=Tr⁡(eβ​Wℓ+e−β​Wℓ)2​Tr⁡eβ​Wℓ=Tr⁡cosh⁡(β​Wℓ)Tr⁡eβ​Wℓ.\mathcal{B}_{\ell}(\beta)=\frac{\operatorname{Tr}\bigl(e^{\beta W_{\ell}}+e^{-\beta W_{\ell}}\bigr)}{2\,\operatorname{Tr}e^{\beta W_{\ell}}}=\frac{\operatorname{Tr}\cosh(\beta W_{\ell})}{\operatorname{Tr}e^{\beta W_{\ell}}}.

This is Estrada’s spectral bipartivity evaluated on the scaled adjacency matrix β​Wℓ\beta W_{\ell}: the numerator collects the weights of even closed walks, while the denominator collects those of all closed walks. The same reduction applies when the diagonal part of the Hamiltonian vanishes.

To summarize, the average sign is fixed exactly by the balance between even and odd closed walks on the HG. It equals unity if and only if the HG is bipartite, it first departs from unity at the order set by the shortest odd cycle, and the vertex degrees enter one order later through their correlation with the local triangle weight.

IX Conclusion & Outlook

In this work, we studied the GS of the J1J_{1}–J2J_{2} HAF Hamiltonian as an optimization problem on the HG, the weighted graph of computational-basis configurations generated by the Hamiltonian’s off-diagonal exchange terms in a fixed-magnetization sector. The HG is the token graph of the underlying lattice, and the identity Hℓ=EF−LℓH_{\ell}=E_{F}-L_{\ell} turns the HAF eigenvalue problem into a spectral problem on it, so that computing the GS energy is equivalent to solving the spectrally relaxed Max-Cut on the HG. At fixed GS amplitudes and with binary phases, the phase-dependent part of the variational energy is a classical antiferromagnetic Ising model on the HG with amplitude-dressed couplings, equivalent to weighted Max-Cut on the same HG.

For weights generated by the exact GS amplitudes, the global minimum of the XY energy lies at a {0,π}\{0,\pi\} assignment, since the GS of the real Hamiltonian can be chosen real, and both the Rank-2 and GW relaxations recover the GS signs with high accuracy. For a nondegenerate GS, the GW relaxation is exact: its minimum equals E0E_{0}, its optimum is the rank-one matrix built from the GS signs, and hyperplane rounding recovers these signs in a time polynomial in the size of the HG.

In VMC with separate amplitude and phase parameters, each phase update is a Rank-2 step for weighted Max-Cut on the HG with weights set by the current amplitudes, so that VMC acts as an evolving Rank-2 relaxed Max-Cut and the phase ansatz inherits its spurious minima and saddle points, consistent with the rugged landscape reported for NQS. Because the MSR solves this Max-Cut for any amplitudes on a bipartite HG, the optimal phases do not move during training, which offers a possible explanation for why sign learning is easier on bipartite lattices. With a real-valued ansatz, a sign prior fixes a cut of the HG in advance, and a good GS energy requires this cut to agree with the GS cut on the high-weight edges, so the signs of the configurations with the largest amplitudes matter most.

On a bipartite HG, the optimal phases come from its two-coloring, which reproduces the MSR, while the odd cycles of the HG, inherited from those of the lattice, prevent any such coloring. The HG edges carry the off-diagonal elements of HℓH_{\ell} as weights; this indicates that a diagonal unitary causes the sector Hamiltonian to be stoquastic if and only if the HG is bipartite, the residual non-stoquasticity constitutes a Max-Cut deficit, and the average sign of the QMC gives the generalized Estrada bipartivity of the HG.

Our results show that the HG viewpoint reveals physics that is hard to see in the lattice formulation of the HAF: the MSR appears as the two-coloring of a bipartite HG, and the sign learning obstruction of frustrated HAFs as odd cycles of the HG and a Max-Cut deficit. This suggests that the same viewpoint can serve as a framework for other strongly correlated systems. A natural next step is the Fermi-Hubbard model. For fixed numbers of up and down electrons, its HG is the Cartesian product of two HGs of the type studied here, one for each spin species, but the hopping amplitudes can carry fermionic signs and the on-site repulsion is not related to the vertex degree, so the identity Hℓ=EF−LℓH_{\ell}=E_{F}-L_{\ell} does not carry over directly. Since the HAF is the strong-coupling limit of the half-filled Hubbard model, the HG studied here is expected to emerge from the Hubbard HG once doubly occupied configurations are eliminated, which would connect the sign structures of the two models.
